10086-the-minute-boys-of-the-mohawk-vall:
James Otis's 1911 boys' book, illustrated by A. Burnham Shute, follows the Minute Boys of the Mohawk Valley in the Revolution. It opens with young soldiers, a powwow, and disappointment, and its frontispiece shows an Indian striding gravely into the encampment.

Otis, author of many boys' histories, writes of frontier warfare, scouting, and loyalty for young readers. The minute boys, ready at a moment's notice, stand between settlements and danger. Boys get a stirring tale of the Mohawk country in wartime, with history woven into adventure. Otis keeps the history close to the boys' own view.
10402-a-man-and-his-money:
Frederic S. Isham published this novel in 1912, with pictures by Max J. Spero. It opens in a run-down music shop, where a scrubby proprietor named Kerry Mackintosh meets a vague visitor who asks, simply, for work. The scene sets a comic, rags-to-riches tone, with money, pride, and chance at its heart.

The visitor's purpose shifts as he advances rather than retreats, and the plot follows how a man and his money shape each other. Isham, author of Under the Rose and Half a Chance, writes in brisk, popular style. Readers get a lively, early twentieth-century tale of fortune, work, and social climbing.
1078-the-scouts-of-the-valley:
Joseph A. Altsheler sends Henry Ware and his friends, young Kentucky scouts, through the forests of the Ohio Valley during the French and Indian War. They track, fight, and outwit French soldiers and their Indian allies, and they learn the woods as their school and their home.

The tale moves from fort to river to ambush with a boy's-book pace, and its heroes are brave, loyal, and quick with a rifle. Altsheler wrote a whole shelf of such frontier tales. The book suits young readers who like clean adventure and the old border wars.
11129-no-and-other-stories-compiled-by-u:
Uncle Humphrey compiled this 1851 children's book, No and Other Stories, for the instruction and amusement of young friends. The preface, signed at Lynn in January 1851, promises lessons on duty: exercise charity as little Willy did, be good sons and daughters, forgive, beware envy, and learn industry. The little word No, though only two letters, keeps readers from sin and misery.

Stories include T. S. Arthur's tale about the word No, Aunt Lissa's Acorn Hollow, and a father's test of his son Caspar, who, woken by a noisy door, cries out in fear and betrays his guilt. Uncle Humphrey promises another volume to any child who can tell him what the book is all about. The collection teaches Victorian morals through short, plain tales for Sunday reading.
12239-dead-men-s-money:
J. S. Fletcher published Dead Men Money in 1920, a detective novel set in an English coastal town. Fletcher, a prolific writer of mysteries, builds his plots from wills, parish records, and local gossip.

Contents run from a one-eyed man and a midnight mission through a red stain and a murdered man. A brass-bound chest, an inquest on John Phillips, signatures to a will, and a salmon gaff follow. A mid-book thread follows a shipwrecked man on a raft, waving to an ugly vessel that alters course toward him. The mystery turns on five hundred a year, an Irish housekeeper, and an ice axe. Fletcher method is steady: clues accumulate until the money trail names the killer.
12945-the-boy-scouts-of-the-geological-s:
Scout Master Robert Shaler's Boy Scouts of the Geological Survey follows Ralph Kenyon, a young trapper who joins a surveying squad. The story opens with Ralph tying a mink to his pack-saddle and figuring what his pelts will fetch, his horse Keno browsing cottonwoods nearby. Camp life, a combat on a cliff, and a night in the woods follow.

A night scene finds Ralph calling to his horse in the dark, Ke-ee-no-o, as a lantern flickers among trees and searchers approach his fire. The scouts learn surveying while solving a camp mystery. The book blends scout craft, field work, and outdoor adventure.
13250-the-chums-of-scranton-high-at-ice-:
Donald Ferguson's The Chums of Scranton High at Ice Hockey, copyright 1919, follows Hugh and his school friends through a season of games, pranks, and a mystery. Chapters run from a bull in the china shop and a hockey match with a scratch seven to a mother's sacrifice. A lively game with Keyport's seven follows, and a safe harbor at last. The boys' tale is brisk and clean.

Hugh argues that Deacon Winslow, a man used to figures, will stick to his statement and clear Nick of a crime. The boy worked at the forge till fifteen minutes after eleven. Later, Hugh spends an evening playing with little Joey, hoping for a clue to the mysterious past of the boy's mother. The book mixes sport, loyalty, and detective work in schoolboy fashion.
1337-shelley:
Sydney Waterlow gives a short, clear life of Percy Bysshe Shelley, the Romantic poet who rebelled against church, king, and custom, and who drowned at twenty-nine off the Italian coast. The book follows Shelley from Eton and Oxford through his loves, his exile, and his great poems.

Waterlow reads Shelley as a poet of rebellion, nature, and love, and his chapters on the poems guide new readers well. The biography is compact and humane. It suits readers who want a first life of Shelley before facing the poems themselves.
13725-stories-from-the-odyssey:
H. L. Havell retold Homer's Odyssey as a set of clear stories for younger readers. Telemachus opens the book, as the young prince seeks news of his father. Then come Odysseus among the Cyclops, Circe, the Sirens, and Calypso, and his long road home to Ithaca. Penelope, loyal through twenty years, waits and tests the returning hero.

Havell keeps Homer's episodes in order and explains Greek customs as he goes. He stresses courage, cunning, and endurance over mere adventure. A verse motto from Tennyson praises strong will under hardship. The retelling suits school readers meeting the epic for the first time. It also works as a refresher for adults who want the story straight.
14331-judith-of-the-godless-valley:
Honoré Willsie wrote this 1922 novel of Lost Chief, a valley in the mountains where faith is scarce. Judith, a girl of pride and independence, stands at its center. A preacher named Fowler brings a log chapel and a first sermon to the valley. Rodeos, wild horses, and a hunt on Lost Chief fill the early chapters. Willsie writes of a hard country and of folk who test each other's creeds.

Judith spars with Fowler over right and wrong, asking how a man dead two thousand years can judge Lost Chief. Fowler answers with the Bible, but Judith calls its prophets tricky and its deeds dirty. Inez Rodman, another voice, says she believes only in kindness and beauty. The novel follows a graduation dance, a post office conference, and a flame in the valley. Its force lies in plain talk about God, morals, and mountain pride.
14473-birds-of-guernsey-1879-and-the-nei:
Cecil Smith, a fellow of the Zoological Society, published this 1879 study of the birds of Guernsey and its neighbors Alderney, Sark, Jethou, and Herm. It was offered as a small contribution to the ornithology of the Channel Islands.

Smith lists breeding and visiting species, notes rarities such as wagtails, and compares his records with earlier writers and local observers. He admits where evidence is thin, as with the yellow wagtail's status. The book remains a careful Victorian faunal list, useful for tracing how island birdlife was understood before modern surveys.
14513-audrey:
Mary Johnston's 1902 Virginia romance follows Audrey, a girl raised in a valley cabin, into the world of Williamsburg planters, storekeepers, and gentlemen. Johnston, author of To Have and To Hold, set the tale in colonial Virginia.

Audrey passes through an orphans' court, Darden's household, and the road to town, meeting Haward and other suitors who drink, duel, and debate honor. Johnston writes with color about dress, houses, and manners. The novel is a romantic historical tale, less famous than its predecessor but equally fond of old Virginia. Johnston later wrote on Virginia history as well as fiction.
14785-down-the-chimney:
Shepherd Knapp's 1921 play for children opens on the roof of a house, just as Mother Goose promised. Jack Frost arrives in white, quick and nimble, complaining that no snow has fallen and no icicle hangs from the chimney, though Christmas is tomorrow.

Mother Cary has already asked him when a real storm will come, and Jack promises to attend to it in good time. The play then follows his storm-making and the household below, with parts written for boys and girls to act and audiences of children to cheer. Dedicated to its first players and trainers, it is a short seasonal entertainment built on snow, mischief and Christmas Eve expectation.
14786-up-the-chimney:
Shepherd Knapp's Christmas play Up the Chimney opens with Mother Goose herself stepping out before the curtain. She promises a Christmas play on Christmas Eve, all about Christmas, and tells children what to expect before the story begins.

The first scene shows a house where a little girl and boy live with their father, a doctor, and their mother. On a very cold evening the children write letters, the mother knits and the father reads his newspaper, while stockings hang by the fireplace. Knapp writes for young performers and young audiences, with clear directions and a warm, old-fashioned Christmas frame.
15356-red-money:
Fergus Hume's 1911 mystery Red Money opens with Mrs. Belgrove, a society lady of sixty, peering through a lorgnette at breakfast and longing to have gypsies tell her fortune. Chapters follow a drama of little things, a wood, an unexpected recognition, secrets, blackmail, and a conspiracy. Miss Greeby turns detective.

Hume, author of The Mystery of a Hansom Cab, writes in a brisk, melodramatic style, with a final surprise and a destined end. The plot turns on money, love, and hidden pasts. Mystery fans will find Red Money a lively, old-fashioned puzzle, full of period manners.
15426-pixy-s-holiday-journey:
Mary E. Ireland translated this German children's story by George Lang, published in 1906 and dedicated to two boys who loved hearing the manuscript read. It follows three schoolboys in the Odenwald country of Hesse-Darmstadt, Fritz, Paul, and Franz, called the three-leaved clover by classmates for their close friendship. All are about eleven, and all attend the same polytechnic school class.

Their holiday journey takes them to inns, a zoo, and a deserted cabin, with trouble for Fritz and for Pixy, earnings, sight-seeing, and a kind welcome along the way. The chapters read like a travel tale for children, full of small adventures and good-natured scrapes. Ireland's translation keeps the story simple and lively, a German holiday book made for English-speaking boys and girls.
15502-the-desert-valley:
Jackson Gregory published this desert novel in 1921, with Hodder and Stoughton in London and Scribner in New York. An opening passage on the desert itself sets the spell. Over wide regions of Arizona and New Mexico lies silence and mystery. The desert swallows travelers and things, then gives back marvels from its depths. That mood governs the whole book.

Chapters follow a bluebird's feather, Superstition Pool, payment in raw gold, and a golden secret, with Sanchia scheming, Howard holding a gulch, and a town being born. Two friends and a girl, a professor, and hidden people add to the tangle. Gregory's desert is both place and force, testing greed, love, and nerve. The novel reads as a strong example of his western romance at its most atmospheric.
1569-the-lily-of-the-valley:
Balzac's tender novel, told as a letter, follows Felix de Vandenesse, a young man of two childhoods: one neglected at home, one saved by love. In the Loire valley he meets Henriette de Mortsauf, a married countess of rare goodness, and his devotion to her becomes the shaping passion of his youth.

Henriette, bound by duty to a sick husband and children, returns a pure, restrained love, and Felix must learn to honour a bond that can never be fulfilled. The valley itself, with its flowers and river, mirrors their feeling. The book is Balzac's most lyrical romance, and one of his most loved.
1628-my-lady-s-money:
Wilkie Collins's My Lady's Money, an episode in the life of a young girl, follows Lady Lydiard, widow of Lord Lydiard, her adopted daughter Isabel Miller. A household of suitors, sisters, and a stud farm owner. When money goes missing, suspicion falls in turn on each member of the house.

Through a country house plot of letters, visits, and a trial of character, Collins keeps the thief's identity in doubt to the end. The novella is short and neatly built. My Lady's Money is a light, enjoyable Collins mystery, perfect for readers who like a domestic puzzle.
16422-the-home-in-the-valley:
Emilie F. Carlen's Swedish novel, brought into English by Elbert Perce in 1854, centers on home life in a valley community. The translator notes Carlen's wide range: in one book she revels in home scenes and people, in another she turns to wilder plots. This tale stays close to house, kin, and daily feeling.

As with her earlier hit One Year of Wedlock, the interest lies in character and domestic ties rather than grand events. The valley setting gives the story its calm, rural frame, while courtship and family duty drive the plot. Readers who like quiet, humane novels of home will find the book gentle and warm.
16445-observations-and-reflections-made-:
Hester Lynch Piozzi records a tour through France, Italy, and Germany in these two volumes, printed in London in 1789. She opens with a Roman custom of criers going before a priest's procession, then turns to the sights, people, and manners she met on the road. The tone is chatty and personal throughout.

Piozzi writes as a lively traveler, not a guidebook compiler, and her notes mix art, food, dress, and social gossip. Readers get an Englishwoman's view of Europe on the eve of revolution. The book is long but easy to dip into, and it still charms with its frank, curious voice.
16890-hetty-wesley:
Arthur Thomas Quiller-Couch wrote this novel of Hetty Wesley, dedicated to Andrew Lang as a good champion of Hetty. It runs in four books plus a conclusion and epilogue, opening at Surat, where a middle-aged man at the East India Company's factory stares out on the river and wharves. A Bible verse on gaining the world and losing one's soul heads the tale.

Quiller-Couch tells of Hetty, sister in the famous Wesley family, caught between faith, family rule, and her own heart. The novel mixes India, England, and chapel life in a long, thoughtful plot. Readers who like historical fiction on faith and family will find a rich, serious tale, well told and full of period detail.
17156-the-soldier-of-the-valley:
Nelson Lloyd's 1904 novel, pictured by A. B. Frost, follows a valley boy through farm work, lots drawn at the plough, and a call to soldier life. Pictures show a welcome home, a tiger story, a prison, a girl on a store porch, and a young colonel wailing in satire. The hero's path runs from boyhood games to war, prison, and a hard-won return.

Lloyd writes in warm, humorous prose with a strong sense of valley speech and home. The tale mixes comedy with the costs of war, and its pictures add charm at each turn. Readers who like early-1900s American novels of youth, war, and homecoming will find a gentle, well-drawn story here.
1748-other-people-s-money:
Émile Gaboriau's novel opens on the quiet Rue Saint-Gilles in the Marais, a street so silent that drums sound loud in it, and follows the Favoral family into ruin. A banker's clerk, a wife who has spent twenty years reading fate on her husband's face. Children who inherit the trouble all figure in a plot of speculation and fraud.

Gaboriau builds the case slowly, through ledgers, loans, and the political events that shake Paris. The title says what the book is about: fortunes made by handling money that belongs to others. It is a financial mystery rather than a murder story, and its suspense comes from watching a respectable household slide toward a crash it cannot name.
17679-the-story-of-a-nodding-donkey:
Laura Lee Hope wrote this make-believe story of a nodding donkey, published in New York by Grosset and Dunlap, with pictures by Harry L. Smith. It belongs to a series that also includes The Story of a Sawdust Doll, The Story of a China Cat, and The Story of a Plush Bear. Chapters open in the Santa Claus shop, then follow a wonderful voyage and the jolly store.

The china cat, the lame boy, and a new home follow, with a flood, a broken leg, and a lonesome donkey ahead. Readers get a toy's-eye tale for small children, gentle and full of shop-window wonder. The book suits young readers who enjoy stories of toys that come alive.
17813-at-ypres-with-best-dunkley:
Thomas Hope Floyd wrote this war book, At Ypres with Best-Dunkley, in the On Active Service series, published in London and New York in 1920 by John Lane. Floyd dedicates the book to all ranks of the Second-Fifth Lancashire Fusiliers who fell at Ypres on July 31, 1917. Chapters open with off to the front, the prison, and the entry of Best-Dunkley.

Millain, the march, and the general's speech follow, with the vale of Acquin and back to the salient ahead. Readers get a battalion-level account of Third Ypres, personal and mournful. The book suits readers of Great War memoirs and of the Lancashire Fusiliers.
18470-the-second-latchkey:
C. N. and A. M. Williamson wrote this mystery novel, published by Doubleday, Page in Garden City, New York, in 1920, with a frontispiece by Rudolph Tandler. The Second Latchkey opens with Annesley Grayle turning from the Strand toward the Savoy, unsure whether she will have courage to walk into the hotel. The dreadful thing she has come to do looms blacker with each step, like opening a lions' cage and stepping inside.

Chapters follow a white rose, Smiths and Smiths, why she came, the great moment, and the second latchkey itself. Later chapters bring the Countess de Santiago, a blue diamond ring, the thing Knight wanted, Annesley remembering, the crystal, and the star sapphire. Readers get a society mystery of jewels, names, and second keys, told with the Williamsons' brisk Edwardian pace.
18626-the-tale-of-major-monkey:
Arthur Scott Bailey wrote this children's animal tale in 1919, with pictures by Lawrence Brehm. It opens in Pleasant Valley, where wild folk whisper of a strange newcomer hanging by his tail in a tree top. Old Mr. Crow scoffs, sure no possum ever came so far north, until Major Monkey himself arrives and stirs up disputes, a plan, and a small war in the woods.

Later chapters follow the Major's schemes, a fast ride, a sweet tooth, capture, and his trip south. Bailey tells the tale in short, chatty chapters with talking beasts and gentle jokes. Young readers get a light woodland adventure with a sly, tricky hero at its core.
18801-green-valley:
Katharine Reynolds wrote this 1919 portrait of a small Yankee town to cure her own homesickness while traveling in South America. Her note tells how, ten thousand miles from home and unable to return for two years, she set down the town she longed to see across the ocean.

The book is dedicated to little one-horse towns where life is sweet and roomy and old-fashioned, where neighbors truly neighbor and days fill with sunshine, rain, and work. Its scenes recall flags on the Fourth of July, picnic baskets, lawns, and porches, all seen through the eyes of one who missed them. The book reads less as a plotted tale than as a fond picture of home, kept warm by distance and longing.
19162-the-lost-valley:
J. M. Walsh wrote this 1921 Australian novel, The Lost Valley, published in Melbourne. It unfolds in three parts: the posthumous puzzle of Mr. Bryce, the adventures of Mr. Abel Cumshaw, and the finding of the lost valley. A thief in the night, a lie, and a cypher drive the opening.

Jimmy Carstairs, explorer by inclination and rolling stone by circumstance, meets a stout, wheezing man on the sands and reads grit in his smile. Pursuit, a hidden valley, and a gathering of eagles follow. Readers get a lively outback mystery of treasure, pursuit, and a valley long lost.
19304-secret-history-revealed-by-lady-pe:
C. N. and A. M. Williamson wrote this 1915 novel, Secret History Revealed by Lady Peggy O'Malley, with a front piece by Clarence Rowe. Peggy, daughter of two or three hundred earls, tells a secret only she, Diana, Major Vandyke, and Captain Eagleston March know, besides presidents and generals who never tell. The unofficial part, she says, is the whole drama.

Peggy, sixteen and a law unto herself, bargains in a curiosity shop for Chelsea lambs while a man of twenty-eight or thirty watches, and she notes his looks in three seconds. Big things grow from tiny ones, like oak from acorn. Readers get a witty society spy romance of youth, secrets, and war.
20292-in-happy-valley:
John Fox, Jr. published In Happy Valley in 1916, tales of the Kentucky mountains. Men, women, children, and babes in arms ride or stroll homeward together. Youths and maids pair off and dally behind the family groups. One rich, dark girl walks alone, last, down the dusty road.

Two young mountaineers squat in shade, whittling, as she passes them. Fox wrote of mountain feuds, love, and codes with a local's love. Happy Valley holds his people in a gentler, more lyrical key. Readers get mountain life told in Fox's warm, musical prose.
20310-hammersmith-fulham-and-putney:
Sir Walter Besant and G. E. Mitton wrote Hammersmith, Fulham, and Putney, a London survey volume. Besant planned a full perambulation of London, parish by parish. Two volumes were to hold that regular, systematic walk through the city. Each parish's history would stand complete in itself under his scheme.

Besant took the keenest interest in that original plan for the survey. Hammersmith, Fulham, and Putney lie along the Thames in west London. Their riverside past mixes villages, great houses, and growing suburbs. Readers get rich local history from two masters of London lore.
21362-the-powder-monkey:
Old seaman Jack Jeens finds a ragged, hungry runaway boy, Phil Leigh, who has fled a beating uncle, in George Manville Fenn's short tale. Jack takes charge of him, but a press gang takes charge of them both, and they land aboard HMS Victory. Phil becomes a powder monkey, carrying powder to the guns.

A fall in the rigging breaks ship's boy Tom Dodds's leg. Phil is set to nurse him as punishment for the chase that caused it. Then comes Trafalgar, and Jack is badly wounded, giving Phil a second patient. Back in Portsmouth, Phil's aunt arrives with an offer that must not cost him Jack.
21470-the-missing-ship-the-log-of-the-ou:
The Missing Ship, Kingston's log of the Ouzel Galley, is set early in the eighteenth century. All its sea work runs under sail or oars, as the preface states. Kingston's copy text was hard to read, with type set close to the fold, yet the tale shines through.

A captain struck down by fever owes his life to his daughter Norah's care. She fans his pale cheek as sick crewmen lie around him. The book runs half as long again as a standard novel, near eighteen hours read aloud. Strong scenes and steady suspense make it one of Kingston's finest long tales.
21672-westminster-abbey:
Mrs A. Murray Smith describes, and John Fulleylove paints, Westminster Abbey in a book reprinted in 1906. Twenty-one full-page pictures in colour show the church inside and out. Smith had written the Annals and the Roll Call of the Abbey.

A walk round the Abbey forms the body of the guide. Plates show Chaucer's tomb, the Confessor's shrine, and the Coronation Chair. Henry the Seventh's Chapel and the tombs of Henry the Third and Queen Philippa appear in colour. The traveller from Whitehall, Smith notes, sees the whole church stretch from east to west, with St Margaret's beside it.
22276-despair-s-last-journey:
David Christie Murray published Despair's Last Journey in 1901, framing it as a tale told on a train. His introduction shows a carriage of tired passengers enduring weary work. A skirmish between the conductor and a fellow passenger comes as a godsend to them. Even after a dirty dollar bill ends the warfare, the voluntary exile in the corner remains worth staring at.

That exile's story fills the book. Murray follows a man who has given up on his old life across countries and chances. The battered portmanteau of the frame tale, plastered with hotel labels, advertises his wandering. It is a story of a soul's last journey out of despair, told with Murray's practised sentiment.
22819-elsie-marley-honey:
Joslyn Gray introduced Elsie Marley to readers in 1918, in a novel built around its young heroine. Gray draws Elsie as a slight, delicate girl. Brown eyes, even features, and pale brown hair falling in paired curls from a clasp at her neck complete the portrait. Her manner is serious beyond her years, with little trace of girlish carelessness.

Gray follows Elsie through the scrapes and duties of a small, watchful world. The period nickname in the catalog title, Honey, hints at the warmth the book aims for. Domestic detail, family feeling, and a young woman finding her footing carry the plot more than shocks do. It is a gentle period novel, best for readers who enjoy character and setting over sensation.
22999-the-ffolliots-of-redmarley:
L. Allen Harker argues about names in The Ffolliots of Redmarley. If a bad name sticks to a boy, one speaker reasons, mustn't the same hold true of a good one? Name a boy Eloquent at birth, the speaker argues, and the odds favor him growing into the name. It's logic, he insists. It's argument, it's logic, that is.

The double-f of Ffolliot signals the family's old-fashioned pride, and Redmarley supplies the village stage. Harker's fiction deals in country houses, clergy, and courtship conducted under watchful eyes. Talk carries her scenes, quick, funny, and pointed beneath the politeness. This novel shows her manner well. Readers who take their social comedy in an Edwardian key, with weddings pending and reputations fragile, will settle in comfortably.
23379-old-mr-wiley:
Greye La Spina wrote this weird tale, first printed in Weird Tales in nineteen fifty one, about a sick boy who lies tossing and moaning until weakness sinks him toward a coma. His father watches in grief, for the boy no longer seems to care much about getting well.

Each night, old Mr. Wiley and his dog come over, or seem to, and Miss Beaver, who tends the boy, must ask whether the callers are real at all. La Spina builds dread from small sights: a thin form under linen, a whispered visit, a doubt that will not settle. Horror readers will enjoy the slow chill, as care for a child meets a haunting that may be kindness, menace, or both.
23538-hugh-selwyn-mauberley:
Ezra Pound wrote this nineteen twenty poem sequence as Hugh Selwyn Mauberley, printed by the Ovid Press, with a Latin motto on heat calling to shade. Part one, Life and Contacts, follows Mauberley through an ode for his tomb, poems on glaucous eyes, Siena and Maremma, Brennbaum, Mr. Nixon, and an envoi dated nineteen nineteen.

Part two, dated nineteen twenty, adds medallions and the famous line on the age demanding, as Pound weighs a poet out of key with his time. For three years, the opening says, Mauberley strove to revive the dead art of poetry and keep the sublime in its old sense, born in a half savage country, out of date. Readers of modern verse will find a sharp, allusive portrait of art, commerce, and a generation that chose prizes over poems.
2362-the-story-of-wellesley:
Florence Converse, a Wellesley graduate, tells the story of her college from its founding by Henry Fowle Durant to its growth into a leading women's institution. The Story of Wellesley covers the campus, its teachers, its students, and the ideals of women's education that shaped it. Converse writes with alumna pride and a historian's care.

The book preserves the early years of a college that helped transform American higher education for women. Its anecdotes of student life charm as well as inform. Readers interested in women's colleges will find a valuable record.
23731-a-martian-odyssey:
Stanley G. Weinbaum's A Martian Odyssey follows the crew of the Ares, the first human beings to set foot on Mars. Chemist Dick Jarvis stretches out in cramped quarters, exulting in air he can breathe after the thin stuff outside. With him are Putz the engineer, Leroy the biologist, and Harrison the astronomer and captain.

Jarvis reaches Mars under twenty years after Doheny's fatal atomic-blast success, and about ten years after Cardoza's moon flight on such a blast. Mars lies flat and desolate under its nearer moon beyond the port glass. Jarvis's tale of what he met out there — strange creatures, stranger logic — made this story a landmark of science fiction, and it still reads fresh today.
24510-the-production-of-vinegar-from-hon:
The Reverend Gerard W. Bancks wrote this short practical treatise, published in a fourth edition at Dartford and London in 1905. It explains how vinegar, or dilute acetic acid, is produced from honey. The book is a working handbook, not a work of theory, aimed at readers who kept bees or made stores at home.

Bancks sets out the process step by step, with the care of a clergyman-naturalist writing for fellow amateurs. The treatise is brief, but it preserves a small domestic craft of its age. Readers interested in beekeeping, old cookery, or household manufacture will find it a curious and charming survival.
24713-stories-of-new-jersey:
Frank R. Stockton wrote these stories of New Jersey, published by the American Book Company in 1896. His preface warns that the volume is not a condensed history of the state, though its stories are arranged chronologically. They are historical incidents, or material connected with New Jersey's history, told as tales.

The first story sends an Italian mariner, John Verrazano, across the Atlantic to the Jersey shore. Later stories follow colonists, patriots, and ordinary folk through the state's past. Stockton, famous for The Lady or the Tiger, tells each tale with humour and clarity. Young readers get a lively introduction to New Jersey.
25713-the-judas-valley:
Gerald Vance writes this science fiction mystery, The Judas Valley, opening with a question: why did everybody step off a ship in a strange valley and promptly drop dead? A well equipped corps of tough spacemen became a field of rotting skeletons in a quiet world of peace and contentment.

Peter Wayne takes a letter from a machine. It is an official note from Lieutenant General Martin Scarborough of the Interstellar Exploration Service. It orders Captain Wayne of the Preliminary Survey Corps to report for assignment to the Lord Nelson. Peter and Sherri must solve the valley's mystery, if they can live long enough.
2604-the-longest-journey:
E. M. Forster divides this novel into three parts: Cambridge, Sawston, and Wiltshire. It opens with a student debate about a cow in a room, a joke that turns into a test of what can be proved. Rickie Elliot, a lame young writer, moves from university friendship to a stifling schoolmaster's life.

Forster follows Rickie toward a half brother he never knew, and toward a choice between convention and truth. The novel is quiet, ironic, and deeply felt, with Wiltshire's downs as a symbol of freedom. It stands as Forster's most personal early book, and a study of a soul finding its way home.
26086-wilmot-and-tilley:
James Hannay's double life, in the Makers of Canada series, pairs Lemuel Allan Wilmot with Tilley, two New Brunswick leaders. Wilmot's chapters follow his ancestry, his early efforts for reform, and his work in the legislature. His mission as delegate to the Colonial Office brought rulings from Lord John Russell on tenure of office and the Reade appointment.

Tilley's half opens with the fight over the duty on foreign timber, which threatened the colonial timber trade and fed the annexation movement of 1848. Tilley backed efforts to guard colonial trade against free trade, and that stand carried him into politics at the St. John election of 1850. Together the lives trace New Brunswick's political growth in the mid-1800s.
26447-the-strange-case-of-mortimer-fenle:
Louis Tracy's 1919 detective novel opens on a bright June morning in 1912, when John Trenholme wakes at the White Horse Inn at Roxton to a bar of sunlight crossing his face. Trenholme soon stands at the center of the strange case of Mortimer Fenley, the murder of a prominent man in the City of London. The affair was later swept from memory by five years of war. Tracy asks whether an evil deed casts its shadow in advance.

Detective Furneaux seeks inspiration, hounds follow a trail, and Scotland Yard is dined and wined as the net spreads. An artist becomes a man of action, side issues multiply, and an ex-convict named Maselli meets Furneaux over drinks at the Regency Café. The settlement closes a tragedy that began with water nymphs and ended in close quarters.
26618-minnie-s-pet-monkey:
Mrs. Madeline Leslie published this volume at Boston in 1864, another of her Minnie and Her Pets books for young readers. Its hero is Jacko, Minnie's sixth pet, a monkey about eighteen inches high with long arms, bright eyes, and a long tail he used like a third hand. Leslie presents him as a pretty little fellow, despite the usual ugliness of monkeys in her telling.

Jacko reached Minnie by sea, bought on the coast of Africa by her uncle Frank's captain from a sailor's hen-coop. Aboard ship, two cats bit off the end of his tail while he slept, leaving him indignant and less proud of it. Later chapters promise Jacko blacking the table and a monkey in church, in tales meant to amuse children while teaching care for animals.
2694-i-and-my-chimney:
Herman Melville wrote this story of a man and his chimney, two grey headed old smokers living in the country. The narrator calls them old settlers, though the chimney settles more every day, and he borrows Cardinal Wolsey's phrase, I and my King, for I and my chimney.

His wife wants the great chimney torn down, and the narrator defends it as a monument, a hearth, and a piece of himself. Melville turns a household quarrel into a comic battle over tradition, comfort, and stubbornness. The tale charms as a small masterpiece of domestic satire.
27522-virginia-of-elk-creek-valley:
Mary Ellen Chase, author of The Girl from the Big Horn Country, published this girls' story with A. L. Burt in New York, by arrangement with the Page Company, in 1917. Chase dedicates it to her mother, a real one, and the chapters follow Virginia's life in Elk Creek Valley.

The joy of anticipation and the arrival lead to a getting-acquainted trip, the Bear Canyon bear, and Jean Macdonald the homesteader. Aunt Deborah Hunter the pioneer, a vigilantes' homestead, a new school-teacher in Bear Canyon, and a cinnamon creek forest ranger follow. An illustration shows Donald pulling in Macduff and yelling to Carver to jump. The story is warm western adventure.
27996-the-free-lances-a-romance-of-the-m:
Captain Mayne Reid wrote The Free Lances, a romance of the Mexican valley, opening on the levee of New Orleans, where a young man reads a poster calling for volunteers for Texas. The poster recalls Santa Anna's treachery, the massacre of Fanning, and the butchery of the Alamo.

The young man answers, I'll go, and is stopped by a giant of six foot six in alligator leather boots, who claims he put the poster up. Reid's tale of Texas volunteers, Mexican war, and frontier adventure follows in the rousing manner of his popular romances for boys.
28057-highways-and-byways-in-surrey:
Eric Parker's Highways and Byways in Surrey, first published in 1908 and reprinted in 1909, is a walking guide to an English county. Parker follows old roads such as the Pilgrims' Way, visits Farnham, Guildford, and Waverley Abbey, and notes churches, inns, and country houses along the way. Hugh Thomson drew the pictures.

Each chapter mixes history, legend, and practical notes on lanes and footpaths, with stories of monks, pilgrims, and local worthies. The tone is leisurely and fond, as if a friend were showing the reader his home county. Walkers and local-history readers still use it as a pleasant companion to Surrey.
28550-song-in-a-minor-key:
C. L. Moore's short vignette Song in a Minor Key gives Northwest Smith, the cool, grey-eyed adventurer of the spaceways, a rare moment of peace. After lonely months and years on alien worlds, Smith lies on a clovered hillside on Earth. He breathes the fragrance of clover warm in the sun.

Earth has outlawed him, and a gun holstered on his chest presses into his ribs. As he lies there he dreams of boyhood: a white-columned house over the hill, familiar voices indoors, and a girl with hair like poured honey. Moore's story is a quiet, wistful pause in a violent career, full of longing for a home Smith can never reclaim.
28616-penshurst-castle-in-the-time-of-si:
Emma Marshall's Penshurst Castle in the Time of Sir Philip Sidney, published by Seeley and Company of London in 1894, sets a tale in Elizabeth's spacious times. Sidney, scholar, poet, statesman, and soldier in a life of thirty-one years, stands at the center. Marshall drew his incidents from H. R. Fox Bourne's memoir, while Mary Gifford, her sister, and the Ratcliffe brothers are invented.

Book 1 opens in 1581, with sisters at the park, a strange meeting, and Whitsuntide scenes. Book 2 moves to Wilton, fire and sword, restoration, and the passing of Philip, closing four years later in 1590. Readers get a historical romance that mixes real fame with imagined village life.
28956-tharon-of-lost-valley:
Vingie E. Roe wrote this 1919 western novel, Tharon of Lost Valley, published by Dodd, Mead in New York, with pictures by Frank Tenney Johnson. Lost Valley lies like a sparkling jewel in the mountain country, a tiny world with its own notions of law, based on primeval instincts. Cattle run by the thousand head, riders jog with six-guns at their hips, and the town of Corvan runs nightly games.

The chapters follow the gun man's heritage, the horses of the finger marks, and the man in uniform. Unbroken bread, signal fires, and a shot in the cañons lead to finger mark and ironwood at last. Roe, author of The Maid of the Whispering Hills, writes a western romance of honor and revenge. Readers get a vivid period tale of a hidden valley and the woman who stands at its heart.
29023-treasure-valley:
Marian Keith wrote this novel, Treasure Valley, published in 1909 by Jennings and Graham, with copyright 1908. The chapters open with the hermit thrush singing, an adventurous expedition, and a first patient, then bring the orphan's arrival, the milkstand club, and a famous practitioner. Later chapters follow the training of the orphans, a strange comradeship, and the secret of the blue silk gown.

The story moves through the coming of Rosalie, a rush for the goal, and a treasure book, toward an elopement, the call of the banshee, and the dawn. Keith, author of Duncan Polite, writes of Canadian country life with warmth and faith. Readers get a gentle, romantic novel of orphans, doctors, and hidden treasure, told in the style of a bygone family favorite.
29266-thurston-of-orchard-valley:
Harold Bindloss wrote this novel, published in New York in 1910 with a frontispiece by W. Herbert Dunton. Bindloss, author of By Right of Purchase and Alton of Somasco, sets the story in Orchard Valley, where Geoffrey Thurston's folly opens the tale. Early chapters follow a disillusion, Geoffrey's first contract, and his progress.

Later chapters bring the legends of Crosbie Ghyll, Millicent's reward, the breaking of the jam, and Geoffrey standing firm. Savine's confidence, a test of loyalty, the work of an enemy, and the bursting of the sluice drive the plot on. Readers get a Bindloss frontier novel of work, rivalry, and reputation, where contracts and character are tested together.
29582-the-tricks-of-the-town-or-ways-and:
Printed in London in 1732 for J. Roberts near the Oxford-Arms in Warwick-Lane, this book exposes the tricks of the town, or ways and means for getting money. It lays bare the lures, wiles, and artifices practiced by the designing and crafty upon the weak and unwary. Its advice is aimed at adventurers and sharers in bubble undertakings, pursuers of pennyworths, and bargain-buyers.

Chiefly collected from papers of the ingenious Mr. John Thomson, scattered between Laurence-Pountney's-Hill and Dover, the book warns how ingots are won only after toils and dangers at inconvenient distance. Readers of con-artist history will find a lively, early guide to London's cheats, bubbles, and bargains.
29588-the-spoilers-of-the-valley:
Robert Watson, author of The Girl of O. K. Valley, wrote The Spoilers of the Valley, printed by A. L. Burt Company of New York with copyright in 1921 by George H. Doran Company. Its heroine's town is described as a merry, happy-go-lucky, scattered little place she loved, ringed by eternal, undulating hills that enclose the valley in a world by itself. Chapters open with a man hunt and a wolf note.

Later chapters visit Pederstone's forge, wayward Langford, a wolf in sheep's clothing, and a bird to pluck. Wild Man Hanson goes wild, and Jim's grand toot closes the fun. Readers of western and valley fiction will find a lively, old-style tale of a valley and its spoilers.
29790-pleasant-journey:
Richard F. Thieme's short tale turns on a midway ride called Journey Home, built by a maker named Jenkins. A buyer named Allenby, who buys for Star-Time, eyes the booth with care. A rough red curtain hides the ride, and crude blue paint spells its name over the door. A big white barn behind holds Jenkins's shop, where each new ride is built and shipped out.

Six thousand dollars is a steep price, and Allenby wants a trial before he pays. The tale's hook lies in its opening riddle, about the hard half of a ticket. It also lies in what a ride home might mean when the ride itself is the show. Thieme keeps it short, wry, and a little uncanny, with the bargain at its heart.
30979-nuala-o-malley:
H. Bedford-Jones wrote this Irish adventure novel, first serialized in four parts in All-Story Weekly from December 30, 1916, to January 20, 1917. The editor's introduction calls it a stirring, entrancing story of Erin when Cromwell was campaigning, when the fighting heritage of Irishmen found vent through sword, ax, and fire. Its hero is Brian Buidh, Brian of the Yellow Hair, and its heroine is Nuala herself.

Part one runs from The Black Woman and The Beginning of the Storm through The Dark Master, Brian leaning on his sword, Yellow Brian riding south, and Brian taking captives. It ends with The Bird Daughter. Part two follows how Brian was netted, the nailing of Brian, Bertragh Castle, and the baiting of Cathbarr. It is a fast, romantic tale of Ireland in wartime, full of swordplay and loyalty.
31173-anxious-audrey:
Mabel Quiller-Couch's children's book, published in London by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge and illustrated by Helen Jacobs, centers on Audrey. She is a child among a lively household of brothers and sisters who has gone to live with her grandmother. The opening chapter finds Mr. Carlyle at the nursery door, listening to Faith sing a lady-bird verse to a wide-awake baby who refuses to sleep.

From that domestic start, the story follows Audrey's worries, muddles, and small adventures in a world of family, servants, and neighbors. Gentle, moral, and full of nursery detail, the book belongs to the Edwardian tradition of wholesome children's tales, written for young readers learning to manage their own anxieties.
3171-in-defence-of-harriet-shelley:
Mark Twain rushes to defend Shelley's first wife in this sharp essay. He jokes that his sins have not earned six years on the bread and water of ordinary literature, while the fat diet of Professor Dowden's Life of Shelley waited for the righteous. For six years he lived in peaceful ignorance, unaware that Shelley's first wife was unfairly treated, as the book shows.

Twain turns his comedy into a case for Harriet. He sifts Dowden's evidence, mocks the biographer's pieties, and restores a wronged woman's standing. The essay shows Twain as literary detective: funny first, but serious in his demand that a life be judged on facts rather than on a poet's later fame.
31722-the-corner-house-girls-in-a-play-h:
Grace Brooks Hill's Corner House Girls in a Play, telling how they rehearsed, how they acted, and what the play brought in, was published at New York by Barse and Hopkins. It was illustrated by R. Emmett Owen. Hill was already the author of The Corner House Girls and The Corner House Girls at School. The frontispiece shows a girl who truly did well in her performance.

The book follows the Corner House girls from first rehearsal through the night of the play itself, and on to what the play earns for them. It is a girls' story of teamwork, stage fright, and success, written for the readers of the Corner House series.
32569-the-luck-of-gerard-ridgeley:
Bertram Mitford's The Luck of Gerard Ridgeley opens aboard the steamship Amatikulu, nearing Natal after a month at sea. Gerard Ridgeley is broad-shouldered and fond of cricket and rowing. Harry Maitland, slighter and eager to seem a man of the world, gazes with him at the green Natal shore, as fellow passengers bound to seek their fortunes.

Both just under nineteen, unrelated, and friends only since boarding, the two young men face a new country where their lines will run on altogether different roads. Mitford follows their luck, work, and choices in Natal, testing which kind of young man prospers when both must shift for themselves.
32583-tape-jockey:
Tom Leahy tells of Arthur Pettigill, a small clerk who tends a room full of tape machines in a rigid, rank-bound state. A reporter named Bartle comes to write about him, and Pettigill talks eagerly, keen to please his betters and to hide any slip.

Pettigill's post is lonely, and his rank shapes every word he dares to speak. As Bartle listens, the clerk's cheerful front starts to crack, and the tale turns on what a low man in a strict system will do to keep his place and his pride.
32744-the-valley:
Richard Stockham tells of a man and a woman who return to Earth after two thousand years among the stars. They sought a world to live on from one end of the galaxy to the other and found none. Earth below lies burned to a cinder, its cities ringed around shrunken seas.

Radio voices greet them with hope almost dead. Yet the man doubts his people would treat a new world better than they treated this one. His companion asks only to stay, and a new birth on Earth, the first in three thousand years, gives the tale its turn. The valley they choose is home itself, greener than any star.
3318-days-with-sir-roger-de-coverley:
Joseph Addison and Richard Steele send the Spectator to the country in these essays, first published in The Spectator. Sir Roger's family opens the set, with Mr Will Wimble, the picture gallery, and a country Sunday. The widow, the chase, and the county assizes follow, before the Spectator's return to town closes the visit.

Sir Roger de Coverley, the kindly, foolish Tory squire, is the essays' center. The Spectator, having often been invited, at last spends a month with him, and reports the household with affectionate irony. Readers meet Augustan England at ease: a squire's house, a village church, and a hunt, all observed by the finest essayists of their age.
33331-an-example-of-communal-currency-th:
J. Theodore Harris's Example of Communal Currency, with a preface by Sidney Webb, sets out the facts about the Guernsey experiment in public money. Published in London in 1911 by the London School of Economics, the pamphlet argues that a community can issue its own currency for public works, and it records how Guernsey did so. Its price, one shilling net, marked it as a tract for reformers.

The pamphlet suits readers of monetary and social history, offering a short, factual case for an idea still debated today. Harris writes plainly, with figures and history rather than theory alone. For students of alternative money, it is a classic source, showing how one small island tried a bold answer to a common problem.
33347-aubrey-beardsley:
Robert Ross's study of Aubrey Beardsley, published in 1909, pairs a life of the brilliant, short-lived artist with sixteen full-page illustrations and a revised iconography by Aymer Vallance. Its frontispiece shows Mrs. Patrick Campbell, now in the Berlin National Gallery, hinting at Beardsley's range as a draughtsman. Ross, a friend of the artist, writes with knowledge and affection.

The book suits readers who love the art of the 1890s, from its black-and-white line to its daring subjects. Its illustrations let Beardsley's work speak, while Ross's text sets it in its time. For students of illustration and decadence, Aubrey Beardsley remains a key source, both a tribute and a careful record of a career cut short.
33517-little-frankie-on-a-journey:
Little Frankie on a Journey, in Mrs. Leslie's books for little children, follows a small boy on his travels. The Little Frankie series, written or edited by A. R. Baker, was sold by all booksellers, alongside question books on Christ's Sermon on the Mount and Sabbath school books. Frankie's journey offers young readers a gentle, moral tale of a child on the road.

The book's charm lies in its simple, Sunday-school tone, where a journey becomes a lesson in kindness, obedience, and trust. Its short chapters suit very young readers and reading aloud. For collectors of children's books, Little Frankie on a Journey is a sweet, old-fashioned volume from a popular series for little ones.
33629-the-autobiography-of-a-monkey:
Albert Bigelow Paine supplies verses for this illustrated 1897 picture book, found and pictured by Hy. Mayer and published by Robert Howard Russell. A monkey narrator tells his own life in rhyme, beginning in an African forest where light plays through the treetops and an elephant king rules the jungle tribes. Born, as he jokes, on the first day of April, he gamboled, swung by his tail, and joined the jungle song.

An old nurse who read his palms foretold travel in many marvelous lands, and the book follows his departure from the forest toward the wider world. Short verses, animal choruses, and plentiful pictures make it a charming survival of late Victorian children's humor, best enjoyed aloud by young readers and their families.
3365-their-wedding-journey:
William Dean Howells sends Basil and Isabel March on their wedding journey in this 1871 novel. They first met in Boston, Howells writes, but the match was made in Europe, where they afterwards saw each other. The outset, a midsummer-day's dream, and the night boat open the trip, with a day's railroading and the enchanted city and beyond.

Niagara, down the St Lawrence, and the sentiment of Montreal follow, with homeward and home, Niagara revisited, and twelve years after their wedding. The novel is Howells's honeymoon book: a young couple learning marriage on the road, in the age of rail and steamboat. Readers get the Marches young, before New York and middle age, and America young with them.
33700-the-modern-woman-s-rights-movement:
Dr. Kaethe Schirmacher surveys the modern woman's rights movement around the world in this 1912 Macmillan volume, translated from the second German edition by Carl Conrad Eckhardt of the University of Colorado. The translator notes that no English book had yet given a history of the movement in all countries. He also warns that Schirmacher, a German advocate actively engaged in propaganda, writes history that is also a political pamphlet. Readers may disagree with her, he says, but will be interested in her point of view.

Her epigraph declares that oppression is opposed to human nature. Eckhardt added footnotes on the American elections of November 1910 and October 1911 and their bearing on woman's rights, plus an index. The survey remains a valuable early international history of feminism, written from inside the movement it describes.
33761-making-money:
Owen Johnson, author of Stover at Yale, writes a novel of wealth, ambition, and love in this 1915 Stokes volume, with eight illustrations by James Montgomery Flagg. Thirty chapters follow Bojo from his arrival through four ambitions and three ways to make money, his father, Daniel Drake the multi-millionaire, the ticker's tyranny, the return of Patsie, a wedding ball.

Later chapters bring paying the piper, facing the truth, hunting a job, Bojo in overalls, a crisis for Doris, a letter to Patsie, a fight in millions, one last chance, a deluge. A frontispiece shows a broken plea that Bojo must marry Doris. Johnson writes a lively, knowing story of American money-making, its temptations, and its costs, with humor and moral bite.
4282-don-rodriguez-chronicles-of-shadow-:
Lord Dunsany wrote this fantasy romance as the chronicles of Don Rodriguez in Shadow Valley. In a playful chronology note, Dunsany admits he cannot date the tale exactly. Magic, he says, melts dates the way acids change metals, so even a careful historian must leave the period vague.

The story follows a young Spaniard of the sword through a shadowed valley of wonders, duels, and strange folk. Dunsany's prose is ornate and musical, and the book belongs with his early fantasies. Readers who like romance touched with magic, told in a deliberately old manner, will find it here.
4555-percy-bysshe-shelley:
John Addington Symonds wrote this short life of Percy Bysshe Shelley for the English Men of Letters series, edited by John Morley. Eight chapters carry the poet from birth and childhood through Eton and Oxford, to life in London and a first marriage, then to a second London residence and separation from Harriet. Later chapters follow life at Marlow and the journey to Italy, residence at Pisa, last days, and an epilogue.

Symonds lists his authorities, from Mrs. Shelley's edition of the poetical and prose works to Hogg's life, Trelawny's records, and Lady Shelley's memorials. He writes as an admirer who still tries to judge Shelley's work and conduct fairly. Readers get a compact, readable introduction to a difficult Romantic poet, useful before tackling the poems themselves, and a clear map of a short, crowded, controversial life.
4695-notes-to-the-complete-poetical-work:
Mary W. Shelley wrote these notes to the complete poetical works of Percy Bysshe Shelley. They open with her preface to the first collected edition of 1839. Obstacles long blocked a perfect edition of Shelley's poems, she says. Those obstacles being happily removed, she hastens to fulfil an important duty. She aims to give productions of a sublime genius to the world, with all possible correctness, and to detail the history as they sprang, living and warm, from his heart and brain.

Mary abstains from remarks on private life, except where passions it engendered inspired his poetry. She says no account of those events has ever approached reality in detail, and she will not colour truth. Errors of action by a man as noble and generous as Shelley, she notes, may be judged with care. Readers get a poet's widow as editor and guide, invaluable for dating and understanding Shelley's poems.
4729-observations-by-mr-dooley:
Finley Peter Dunne gathers Observations by Mr. Dooley, in the voice of an Irish-American saloon keeper. Its contents run from a little essay on books, the law's delays, and Sherlock Holmes. They go on to international amenities, art patronage, immigration, White House discipline, money and matrimony, and Prince Henry's visit and reception. Cuba versus beet sugar and bad men from the West follow.

Later pieces cover the Philippine peace, soldier and policeman, and King Edward's coronation. Home life of geniuses, reform, and administration lead to work, sport, and the names of a week. Newport, Arctic exploration, machinery, and swearing follow. The war game and newspaper publicity close the set, with rights of women, avarice, and gratitude. The opening essay has Hogan saying man's first acts, after learning to kill animals for food and clothing, included manufacturing literature. Readers get commentary on America at the turn of the century.
5098-lives-of-the-english-poets-waller-m:
Samuel Johnson's Lives of the English Poets, in this volume on Waller, Milton, and Cowley, begins with the booksellers' bargain itself. Johnson agreed to write little lives and little prefaces for a little edition of the English poets. His conscience pricked him because the bargain was struck on Easter Eve, March 29, 1777.

Bookseller Edward Dilly told Boswell the history. An Edinburgh edition of poets, printed by the Martins and sold by Bell in London, had prompted the London trade to commission Johnson's lives. The volume that follows judges three poets with Johnson's famous severity and sense. Readers get literary biography at its founding, where criticism and character meet.
5343-rainbow-valley:
Lucy Maud Montgomery's Rainbow Valley returns to Ingleside, where Anne's children and the manse children play in the valley of their name. The book carries a dedication to Goldwin Lapp, Robert Brookes, and Morley Shier. The book opens with home again and sheer gossip.

Chapters follow the Ingleside children, the manse children, and the advent of Mary Vance, who stays at the manse, with Miss Cornelia intervening in a fishy episode. Readers get a warm sequel to Anne's story, in which a new generation's mischief and tenderness fill the valley Montgomery loved.
5738-cappy-ricks-or-the-subjugation-of-m:
Peter Kyne introduces Alden Ricks, called Cappy Ricks, as master of many ships and skipper of none, a Pacific Coast lumber and shipping character. A psychologist might call him an individualist, Kyne notes, but his associates simply call him a character. Chapters follow the man from blue water, the Blue Star flag, bad news from Cape Town, Matt Peasley assuming office, and a wordy war at a dollar a word.

The book gives a comic business saga in which an old shipping magnate bends younger men to his will through bluff, wit, and stubbornness. The battle of Table Bay, telegrams, and campaigns give the story sea flavor and boardroom bite. Kyne's humor suits readers who enjoy character-driven tales of commerce, ships, and strong personalities clashing over profit and pride.
6016-roast-beef-medium-the-business-adve:
Edna Ferber follows Emma McChesney, a traveling businesswoman, and opens with a philosophy served at life's dining table. Roast beef, medium, is safe, sane, and sure, yet a soft voice purrs temptations: tongue in aspic, chicken pie country style, eggs Benedictine, flaked crab with Russian sauce.

Emma, unimpressed by fine airs, chooses the plain, steady course over light and tempting novelties. Ferber writes with humor about salesmanship, hotels, and a woman holding her own in a man's trade. The foreword turns a menu into a moral, praising substance over show in business and in life.
6160-fletcher-of-madeley:
Brigadier Margaret Allen writes Fletcher of Madeley for the Salvation Army. She traces John Fletcher from castle and manor house through early adventures and a sweet girlhood to a new life given up to the fight. Turned from home, he becomes Tern Hall tutor and vicar of Madeley.

Chapters follow an alarmed parish, the vicar's sermons, scanty encouragements, an orphan home, a seeker after God, sanctified letter-writing, and the college of Trevecca. Failing health, Lake Leman shores, a wonderful wedding, and life at Madeley close the tale, with extracts from letters and writings. Commissioner Railton introduces the book.
6325-a-fool-and-his-money:
George Barr McCutcheon lets his narrator confess at once that his Uncle Rilas called him a fool. It happened in his mother's presence, when he was least able to admit it and most arrogant in asserting his own wisdom. He was a freshman in college then, an excuse for both of them. Another uncle suffered in silence. He admitted only, as if it were a crime, that he too had been in college and knew less on leaving than on entering, after twenty-three years on the faculty.

The chapters that follow are told in the first person, each a fresh folly: defending himself, defending his property, conversing with a mystery, becoming an ancestor, meeting the foe and falling. Matrimony is discussed, visitors received, diplomacy tried, and money lent. McCutcheon writes a comic memoir of a young man learning, expensively, that money and sense do not travel together.
6355-locusts-and-wild-honey:
John Burroughs, in the fourth volume of his writings, warns that his title is mostly allegory, not literal description. Yet it suggests the wild and delectable in nature, the free harvests the wilderness offers an observing eye. The pastoral bees open the book, going forth in spring like the dove from Noah's ark and returning with golden pollen on each hip, first tasted from maple sap at the spiles.

Sharp eyes, strawberries, rain signs, speckled trout, birds and birds, a bed of boughs, and birds' nesting follow, with the halcyon in Canada to close. Burroughs writes as a walker and watcher, fond of bees, trout streams, and ledges, and his prose turns field notes into meditation. The book is nature writing at its most companionable, where a hive, a stream, and a nest become lessons in attention.
6370-the-story-of-the-odyssey:
The Reverend Alfred J. Church retells the Odyssey for young readers, beginning after Troy's fall, when chiefs sail home under heaven's wrath. One is shipwrecked, another slain by a false wife in his palace, others find home troubled and changed. Ulysses wanders farthest and suffers most, still far from Ithaca after nearly ten years, while gods gather on Olympus, all but Poseidon, gone to feast.

Athene counsels, assemblies meet, Nestor and Menelaus tell tales, and Ulysses rides a raft to Nausicaa, Alcinous, and the Phaeacians. Cyclops, Aeolus, Laestrygons, Circe, dwellings of the dead, sirens, Scylla, and the oxen of the sun follow, with Ithaca, Eumaeus the swineherd, and home at last. Church keeps Homer's shape in plain prose, with pronunciation notes, for readers meeting the epic first.
6684-uneasy-money:
Wodehouse opens in June in London, where Lord Dawlish stands at the Bandolero Restaurant, gazing up Shaftesbury Avenue with a wistful frown. He has no secret sorrow; he is merely passing time in mental golf while Claire Fenwick keeps him waiting. The joke, that a lord's chief care is a golf ball, sets the comic tone.

Money, love, and a tangle of wills soon pull Dawlish into Wodehouse's usual merry maze. The prose is light, the talk bright, and the scrapes mounting. Uneasy Money is a classic Wodehouse farce, where wealth causes more trouble than want, and love sorts it out in the end.
6705-mrs-shelley:
Lucy Madox Rossetti writes the life of Mary Shelley, wife of the poet, in a volume dated 1890. Her preface thanks earlier students of Shelley, not least her own husband, for loving and truthful research, and says she only had to compare, sift, and use known material with judgment. For years after Shelley's death, new papers placed in her hands back every new claim.

The life that follows covers Mary as writer, wife, widow, and mother, through Frankenstein's fame and later sorrows. Rossetti's tone is careful and fair. Mrs. Shelley is a solid, early biography of a major writer, drawn from documents rather than from gossip.
7948-abbotsford-and-newstead-abbey:
Washington Irving paired two travel sketches in this volume, both written from visits he made years earlier. The first recalls his arrival at Abbotsford on August 29, 1817, when he travelled from Edinburgh to meet Sir Walter Scott at his Border home. The second describes Newstead Abbey, the Nottinghamshire house once owned by Lord Byron, with its gardens, servants, old customs, and local legends.

Irving warns that his notes were scanty and his memory fallible, so the pieces read as personal recollection rather than guidebook fact. He lingers on conversations, rooms, walks, and the lore attached to each place. For readers of Scott and Byron, the book offers a friendly eyewitness view of two famous literary homes as they looked in the early nineteenth century.
8580-reminiscences-of-samuel-taylor-cole:
Joseph Cottle, the Bristol bookseller who published the young Romantics, writes these memories near the end of a long life, having outlived almost all his early friends. He looks back on Samuel Taylor Coleridge and Robert Southey as he knew them: their talk, their plans, their quarrels, and their daily habits. The tone is solemn and personal, a survivor settling accounts with the past.

Cottle's value lies in closeness: he was there when poems were drafted, debts mounted, and friendships strained. His pages preserve letters, anecdotes, and judgments that no later biographer could recover firsthand. For readers of Coleridge and Southey, the book is a rich, if partisan, witness, best read beside modern lives of the poets, which test Cottle's memories against other evidence.
9362-birds-of-prey:
Mary Elizabeth Braddon wrote this sensation novel of fatal friendship, poison, and greed. Its first book opens in a house in Bloomsbury, where Philip Sheldon reads the Lancet and a perplexing illness strikes. Letters from an insurance office and Mr. Burkham's doubts deepen the plot. A captain soon demands to be taken straight to her, claiming to be her father.

Later books follow two Macaires, a golden temple, an easy descent, and heaped-up riches, through marriages, compacts, and watches. Braddon spins her web with relish. The novel remains a gripping Victorian thriller of money, murder, and family ruin.
9787-in-the-valley:
Harold Frederic wrote In the Valley in 1890, a novel of the Mohawk Valley during the American Revolution. Frederic began the tale after years of preparation, hoping to please a venerable friend who inspired its first idea. The valley's farms, forts, and frontier wars form the story's ground. Settlers, soldiers, and native allies cross its pages.

The novel follows valley folk through raids, loyalties, and loves, as revolution divides neighbors. Frederic writes with care for place and period speech. A reader gets a sturdy historical novel of New York's frontier war, rich in valley life and Revolutionary strife.
9794-calvary-alley:
Alice Hegan Rice, famed for Mrs. Wiggs of the Cabbage Patch, wrote Calvary Alley in 1917, a novel of poor children and city courts. Chapters follow the Snawdors and Clarkes at home, a juvenile court, probation, and an eviction. Butternut Lane, ambition, and buttons mark the children's rise. A princess comes to grief, and the state takes a hand.

Later chapters bring a signal tower, Calvary Cathedral, and a first case, as Nance comes into her own. Rice writes with warmth for Kentucky folk and city poor alike. A reader gets a humane, old-style novel of childhood, courts, and second chances, dedicated to Kentucky writers.
9840-vivian-grey:
Benjamin Disraeli, Earl of Beaconsfield, wrote Vivian Grey in 1826-27, his first work of fiction, published when he was barely twenty-one. The publisher's note places Disraeli among Bulwer, Dickens, and Thackeray, with Scott's later years as backdrop. Vivian Grey and Sybil mark his truly creative period, while Lothair and Endymion add only old age's changes. His style dates from that early time.

The novel follows young Vivian's schemes in high society and politics, with wit and ambition. Disraeli writes with dandy brilliance and social bite. A reader gets the dazzling debut of a future prime minister, and a portrait of Regency ambition.
9909-nightmare-abbey:
Thomas Love Peacock's short novel, published in 1818, gathers a party of gloomy philosophers and poets at Nightmare Abbey, a gloomy country house. Its young owner, Scythrop, nurses a grand, melancholy view of life and love.

Over long dinners and walks, the guests argue about poetry, politics, and the ruin of the world, each more gloomy than the last. Peacock gently mocks the fashionable despair of his age, including friends like Shelley and Byron in disguise. It is a witty, compact satire, still funny for readers who know the Romantics. Peacock's circle of friends included Shelley, whose gloom he gently mocked.
9988-amarilly-of-clothes-line-alley:
Belle K. Maniates's 1915 novel introduces Amarilly, a girl of Clothes-Line Alley, whose work, caprices, and charm fill the book's illustrations. One picture shows a man gazing into her intent eyes with adoration, another shows her work on display, and a third calls her the little peacemaker.

Amarilly's story turns on her efforts to make her way, to be nice to Mr. St. John, and to smooth the troubles around her. Maniates, author of David Dunne, writes warmly about a spirited girl in a poor city neighborhood. Readers get a sunny, old-fashioned heroine whose kindness is her strength.
a-fool-and-his-money:
George Barr McCutcheon lets his hero narrate in the first person, and the chapter titles keep his voice. They run: I Make No Effort to Defend Myself, I Defend My Property, I Converse with a Mystery, I Become an Ancestor. A young American writer, suddenly richer than he meant to be, has bought a castle on the Danube to work in peace. The neighbors will not leave him in it.

A mysterious woman on a balcony, visitors, dinner invitations, and requests for loans besiege him in turn, until he is forced into being a hero and informed that he is in love. McCutcheon, the author of Graustark, writes light romance at a trot, with castles, counts, and comedy.
a-man-and-his-money: Frederic Stewart Isham tells of a man and his money through Mr. Heatherbloom. The hero faces many creditors with a carefree, if artificial, jocularity. A run down music emporium and its scrubby proprietor open the tale. Isham writes a comic novel of debt, bluff, and fortune. The comic tale keeps its pace from first page to last.
abbotsford-and-newstead-abbey: Washington Irving visits Abbotsford and Newstead Abbey in this volume, promising an account from travelling notes he calls scanty and vague and a memory extremely fallacious. Late on August 29, 1817, he reached Selkirk from Edinburgh, chiefly to see the mighty minstrel of the north, armed with a letter of introduction from Thomas Campbell the poet. Newstead brings an abbey garden, Plough Monday, old servants, superstitions, Annesley Hall, the lake, and Robin Hood's Sherwood.
amarilly-of-clothes-line-alley: Belle Kanaris Maniates introduces Amarilly of Clothes-line Alley, a spirited girl growing up in a poor city neighbourhood. The novel follows Amarilly's family, friends, and first steps toward a better life, with humour and warmth. Illustrated by J. Henry, it is a cheerful American story of pluck, kindness, and hope among working folk.
at-ypres-with-best-dunkley:
Thomas Hope Floyd wrote this war memoir for the On Active Service series, published at London in 1920. Floyd served as an officer in the Second-Fifth Lancashire Fusiliers and dedicates the volume to all ranks of the battalion who fell at Ypres on the thirty-first of July 1917. His title names Best-Dunkley, the commanding officer the men followed into that battle.

Diary entries record dug-outs in the Ramparts, dinners at Potijze, and companies moving out by night toward Goldfish Chateau. Shells fly over an otherwise peaceful view of the Salient, and officers share what room the ramparts allow. Floyd writes plainly, without heroics, leaving a battalion-level record of the opening of the Third Battle of Ypres and its cost.
audrey:
Mary Johnston published this colonial Virginia romance in 1902, with illustrations by F. C. Yohn. Johnston had already won a wide public with To Have and to Hold, and she returned to the same early Williamsburgh world. Her heroine is Audrey, an orphan girl raised by the rough Darden, whose cabin in the valley opens the tale.

Gentleman Haward meets Darden's Audrey and finds her proud as a princess though she owns nothing. Johnston follows her through the orphan's court, the road to Williamsburgh, and drawing-room tests where money is refused as an insult to a gift. Planters, servants, and grandees circle the girl whose quick wit and courage keep winning protectors. The book is a costume romance of rank, gratitude, and love in the young colony.
birds-of-guernsey-1879-and-the-neighbour:
Cecil Smith published this account of the birds of Guernsey and the neighbouring islands — Alderney, Sark, Jethou, and Herm — with R. H. Porter of London in 1879. Smith, a fellow of the Zoological Society, calls it a small contribution to the ornithology of the Channel Islands. His preface grants that Guernsey cannot match Lundy's gannets, the Scillies, or Gätke's famous list for Heligoland, yet insists its avifauna is far from devoid of interest.

Migration timing gets the careful treatment. A few migratory flocks probably rest briefly in the islands on their way north or south. The earliest arrivals and latest laggers belong to such passing flocks, Smith reasons, while regular summer residents arrive a little later and leave a little earlier. Species by species, with dates, nests, and the records of Miss Carey and other local observers, Smith builds the first real list for the islands.
birds-of-prey:
M. E. Braddon published this sensation novel in 1867, in four books with titles like chapter headings to a sermon on greed. Fatal Friendship opens it in a house in Bloomsbury, where Philip Sheldon reads the Lancet and a perplexing illness begins. The Two Macaires follows, then Heaping Up Riches, and last Valentine Hawkehurst's Record, the confession that explains the crimes.

Sheldon's schemes reach from London to dull provincial Ullerton, whose commercial centre life seems desolation to a man used to Paris. A narrator travels by coach to Spotswold in a cramped and painful position, suspecting nothing of his friend and benefactor's designs. Braddon builds the novel on a doctor who poisons for legacies and a clerk who keeps the record: birds of prey in broadcloth, circling inheritances.
britannica-1911-aberdovey:
Aberdovey receives a village entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, inside a shared chunk of text. The Merionethshire seaside village stands on the Dyfi estuary's north bank, where the river forms the county frontier. Its 1,466 folk in 1901 lived by the Cambrian railway trade.

Views cross to Snowdon, Cader Idris, Arran Mawddy, and Plynlimmon from the shore. A ferry takes travellers over the mile-broad Dyfi to Borth sands and the Aberystwyth road. Drowned bells give the place its song fame: Seithennin's drunken fault, in the old tale, let the sea form Cardigan Bay and sink them. Health and bathing close the entry's case for the resort, small but sung across Wales.
britannica-1911-abomey:
Abomey receives a town entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, inside a shared chunk of text. The town captained the ancient kingdom of Dahomey in West Africa and now sits in the French colony of that name. Rail joins it to the seaport Kotonu, seventy miles south.

A mud wall of six miles' girth, six gates, and a ditch of prickly acacia guarded the royal town. Villages, palaces, a market, and barracks filled the ring on a rolling plain. King Behanzin, beaten by France, burned Abomey in November 1892 and fled north. French rule rebuilt it, sank artesian wells for water, and brought the railway in 1905. Some 15,000 folk live there, the entry counts.
britannica-1911-airey-richard-airey:
Airey, Richard Airey, Baron Airey, a British general of 1803 to 1881, is given his own article within the hosted text of the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Son of Lieutenant-General Sir George Airey, he entered the army in 1821 and became a captain in 1825. Staff service followed in the Ionian Islands and in North America under Lord Aylmer.

At the Horse Guards he became military secretary to Lord Hardinge, then went east in 1854 as quartermaster-general to Lord Raglan in the Crimea. The army judged him the best soldier on Raglan's staff, yet the public blamed his department for the commissariat's failures. An inquiry he demanded cleared him completely, though he never recovered from the unjust persecution. He later governed Gibraltar, served as adjutant-general, reached full general, and chaired the celebrated Airey commission on army reform.
britannica-1911-alderney:
Alderney, one of the Channel Islands, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Called Aurigny in French, it is the northernmost of the group's principal islands and belongs to England. It lies nine miles west of Cape La Hague on the Normandy coast. The island is about three and a half miles long and a mile broad, holding 2,062 people in 1901.

The strait between Alderney and the cape, called the Race of Alderney, is dangerous in storms, since rocks, reefs, and conflicting currents crowd it. The scattered French fleet escaped through it after La Hogue in 1692. The narrower Swinge channel to the west is dangerous too. Sandstone, granite, and porphyry form the island, trees are scarce, and wells supply most water. The town of St Anne stands near the centre, overlooking the harbour at Braye on the north coast.
britannica-1911-anglesey:
Anglesey, or Anglesea, is an insular county of northern Wales, separated from the mainland by the Menai Straits. Telford's suspension bridge crossed those straits in 1826, and Stephenson's tubular railway bridge followed in 1850. The county covers about 276 square miles in the diocese of Bangor. The land is mostly flat, the climate humid, and rising water generally scarce.

Very old pre-Cambrian rocks form the island's foundation, surfacing in western, central, and eastern districts as schists and slates, with a belt of granite to the north-west. A few lakes dot the interior, and hills such as Holyhead Mountain give modest relief. The entry judges the soil poor compared with its old fertility and finds few industries. A closing history follows the island from Roman traces at Holyhead through devastating Danish raids, notably in 853, with Welsh authorities cited for the annals of Gwynedd.
britannica-1911-bailey:
Bailey, in castle building, is the open space between the inner and outer lines of a fortification, the court enclosed by the walls. Some castles hold more than one such court, an Inner Bailey and an Outer Bailey, as the names still kept at several English sites show.

Word origin is disputed in the entry itself. Some take bailey as a corruption of ballium. Others derive it from French baille, tied to bataille, battle. Soldiers were drilled in battle order on that ground. London and York keep an Old Bailey. Colchester keeps an Upper and a Nether Bailey. The term lives on in town names. It long outlasted the walls it once named.
britannica-1911-ballymoney:
Ballymoney is a market town of County Antrim, Ireland, 53 miles north-west of Belfast by the Northern Counties railway. The Ballycastle railway joins the main line here. Its urban district held 2,952 people in 1901.

Trade in the town was sound. Brewing, distilling, and tanning went on, along with the linen making common across the county. Soap, candles, and tobacco were also made, and the town served as a centre for farm trade round about. The 1911 Britannica entry adds a note of outside interest: near Dervock, a cottage bore an inscription marking it as the home of ancestors of William McKinley, president of the United States.
britannica-1911-bardsey:
