Bardsey is an island at the northern end of Cardigan Bay, off the Lleyn coast of north Wales, in Carnarvonshire. Its Welsh name, Ynys Enlli, means isle of the current, and the sound between it and Aberdaron point is some four miles wide. High cliffs guard its north-west side.

The island runs about two miles long, with some 370 acres, a third of them hilly, growing barley and oats. A fairly deep harbour lies on the south-east. Ruins of St Mary's abbey tower stand on the north-east, and the inhabitants, farmers and fishermen, were Dissenters with no Anglican church. The 1911 Britannica entry recalls St Dubricius, who made the sanctuary famous and died here in 612, and the monks from all England buried on the isle.
britannica-1911-barnard-george-grey:
George Grey Barnard (born 1863) was an American sculptor, born at Bellefonte, Pennsylvania, on 24 May 1863. He first studied at the Art Institute of Chicago, then worked from 1883 to 1887 in the Paris studio of P. T. Cavelier. He lived in Paris for twelve years in all, returning to America in 1896.

His first exhibit at the Paris Salon of 1894 scored a great success. The 1911 Britannica entry lists his principal works. Among them are The Boy and Cain, the latter later destroyed. Brotherly Love and the allegorical Two Natures, now in the Metropolitan Museum in New York, are named. So are The Hewer at Cairo, Illinois, and Great God Pan in Central Park. It also notes his sculptural decorations for the new state Capitol at Harrisburg, Pennsylvania.
britannica-1911-barnsley:
Barnsley is a market town and municipal borough in the West Riding of Yorkshire, England, fifteen miles north of Sheffield. Called Black, or properly Bleak, Barnsley, it grew from 35,427 people in 1891 to 41,086 in 1901. Five railway companies serve it, and it stands on rising ground west of the river Dearne, in the parish of Silkstone, which gives its name to important collieries.

Iron and steel making and the weaving of linen and other cloth lead its industries, with bleachfields, printfields, and dyeworks besides. The 1911 Britannica entry notes the church of St Mary, built in 1821 on an early site. It also notes a free grammar school dating from 1665. A public park was given in 1862 by the widow of Joseph Locke.
britannica-1911-batley:
Batley is a municipal borough in the West Riding of Yorkshire, England, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies within the parliamentary borough of Dewsbury, eight miles south-south-west of Leeds, and is served by three railways. Its people numbered 30,321 in 1900, and its area was 2039 acres. The church of All Saints is mainly Perpendicular in style and holds fine woodwork, much of it from the 1600s, and good tombs.

Cloth is the town's life. Batley is a centre of the heavy woollen trade, with wide making of army cloths, pilot cloths, druggets, and flushings. The working up of old cloth as “shoddy,” new yarn spun from pulled waste, is done on a large scale. Iron foundries, machine works, and stone quarries add to the trade. The town lies on the south-west Yorkshire coalfield, and many pits work in the district around it.
britannica-1911-baxter-robert-dudley:
Robert Dudley Baxter (1827–1875), an English economist and statistician born at Doncaster, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was educated privately and at Trinity College, Cambridge. He studied law and entered his father's firm of solicitors, Baxter and Co., staying with it till his death. Though a careful man of business, he belonged to the Statistical Society and other learned bodies. Through them he did much useful work in economics.

Figures were his chosen tools. His chief writings deal with the budget and the income tax, with railway growth and its results, and with the national income of the United Kingdom. Later books took up taxation, the national debts of the world, and local government. He also wrote on politics: the volunteer movement, the redistribution of seats in Parliament, English parties and conservatism, and the political progress of the working classes.
britannica-1911-bayonne-new-jersey:
Bayonne is a city of Hudson county, New Jersey, on the peninsula between New York harbour and Newark Bay. It adjoins Jersey City and faces Staten Island across the narrow Kill van Kull. Its people numbered 19,033 in 1890 and 55,545 by 1910, on about four square miles of land.

Two railways and electric lines serve the city, whose chief buildings include the city hall, library, post-office and hospital. Bayonne shares in the trade of the port of New York and ranks high among New Jersey factory towns. Standard Oil’s huge refineries there make it the main oil shipping point on the Atlantic coast.
britannica-1911-belley:
Belley is a town of eastern France, capital of an arrondissement in Ain, fifty-two miles south-east of Bourg. It sits on vine-covered hills at the south end of the Jura, three miles from the Rhone’s right bank. In 1906 the town held 3,709 people and the commune 5,707.

The cathedral of St Jean is mostly modern, save a choir of 1413, and the town is a bishop’s seat with a prefect and a court. Morocco leather goods and lithographic stone from local quarries are its trades, with dealings in cattle, grain, wine and truffles. Belley is Roman in origin, became a bishopric in the 400s, and passed from Savoy to France in 1601.
britannica-1911-bellows-henry-whitney:
Henry Whitney Bellows (1814–1882) was an American clergyman born in Boston. Harvard gave him his degree in 1832 and its divinity school trained him by 1837. After a short pastorate at Mobile, he took the First Congregational, or Unitarian, church in New York in 1839 and held it for life.

Bellows led American Unitarians as preacher, lecturer and editor of The Christian Inquirer. When the Civil War broke out he planned the United States Sanitary Commission and presided over it until 1878. He also helped found the Union League Club and the Century Association, planned Cooper Union with Peter Cooper, and led the first Civil Service Reform Association.
britannica-1911-bermondsey:
Bermondsey, a south-eastern borough of London bounded by the Thames, Deptford, Camberwell, and Southwark, is described in the 1911 Britannica with a 1901 population of 130,760. It was a poor, working district, its people employed in leather factories, other works, and the Surrey Commercial Docks and riverside wharves.

The entry notes the Rotherhithe Tunnel, opened in 1908, the older Thames Tunnel of 1843, and Southwark Park's 63 acres. Bermondsey's name, already in Domesday, points to its marshy, island past. A Cluniac monastery stood there from 1082, and Jacob's Island, in the borough, was the scene of Bill Sikes's death in Dickens's Oliver Twist.
britannica-1911-bingley:
Bingley is a market town in the West Riding of Yorkshire, England. It stands on the river Aire, in the Otley parliamentary division. The Midland railway serves the town. The 1911 Britannica entry gives 18,449 people in the urban district in 1901. All Saints church is a good Perpendicular building, though much restored over time. The town's large working population is busy chiefly in two textile trades named in the entry.

Those trades are worsted and cotton manufacture. Mills in the town employ most of its people, the entry implies throughout. The district around Bingley is populous as well. Yet the natural beauty of the Aire valley is not greatly spoiled by the industry, the entry adds. The account is a short gazetteer note of a few lines. Church, population, railway, and the two cloth trades carry its whole picture of the town.
britannica-1911-binmaley:
Binmaley is a town in the province of Pangasinan, on Luzon in the Philippine Islands. It stands on the delta of the Agno River, about five miles west of Dagupan. Dagupan is the north terminus of the Manila and Dagupan railway. The town's population in 1903 was 16,439. Fisheries of importance work from the town, the 1911 Britannica entry says. Salt making is another named trade of the place.

Pottery, roofing of nipa leaves, and nipa wine are also made at Binmaley. Rice and coconuts are the chief farm products of the town's land. The entry is a brief gazetteer note of a few lines in total. It gives the delta position, the census figure, and the trade list. No church, history, or language note appears in the text. Fish, salt, and rice define the town in this short record.
britannica-1911-bishop-sir-henry-rowley:
Sir Henry Rowley Bishop (1786–1855) was an English musical composer, born in London on 18 November 1786. He trained under Francisco Bianchi. In 1804 his piece Angelina was performed at Margate, when he was just eighteen. A ballet, Tamerlan et Bajazet, succeeded at the King's Theatre in 1806. His first opera, The Circassian's Bride, burned with Drury Lane theatre after one performance in 1809. The Maniac at the Lyceum in 1810 established his reputation instead.

He became composer to Covent Garden for three years. Guy Mannering, The Slave, and Clari count among his stage successes there. Clari brought in the famous air Home, Sweet Home in 1822. The 1911 Britannica entry marks his Aladdin of 1825 as the close of his opera career. He helped direct the new Philharmonic Society from 1813. Knighted in 1842, he was the first musician to receive that honour. He died in poor circumstances in April 1855.
britannica-1911-blakeney-william-blakene:
William Blakeney (1672–1761), later Baron Blakeney, was an Irish-born British soldier who rose very late after long neglect. Born at Mount Blakeney in Limerick, he chose arms over politics, led tenants against the Rapparees at eighteen, and won his commission at the siege of Venlo in 1702. He served through Marlborough's campaigns.

For years after Utrecht he went unnoticed and was sixty-five before he became a colonel. Then promotion came fast. He defended Stirling Castle against the Highlanders in 1745 and became lieutenant-governor of Minorca. The closing pages tell of 1756, when French forces landed on Minorca and Blakeney, left in sole command, faced the attack in the opening of the Seven Years' War.
britannica-1911-blarney:
Blarney is a small town in County Cork, Ireland, 5 miles north-west of Cork city, with 928 people in 1901. It had a large tweed manufacture. Yet the place is famous worldwide for a word and a stone, not for cloth.

The word blarney has passed into English for a smooth, coaxing way of talking said to be typical of the Irish. Kissing the Blarney Stone in the castle is said to give that gift, though the entry admits the belief's origin is unknown. The castle, built about 1446 by Cormac McCarthy, had walls up to 18 feet thick. One story traces the word to McCarthy's own delays, won by persuasion and promises, when he was pressed to surrender the castle.
britannica-1911-bolton-abbey:
Bolton Abbey is a village in the West Riding of Yorkshire, 22 miles north-west from Leeds, named, not quite rightly, for Bolton Priory. The ruins stand near the right bank of the upper Wharfe, in a valley thickly wooded and tightly closed by hills. They rank among the most beautifully set ruins in England.

The church nave survives whole, in Early English and Decorated work, while transepts and choir are ruined. A priory was first founded at Embsay in 1120 by William de Meschines and Cicely de Romili. Their daughter Alice moved it to Bolton in 1151, giving the manor to the monks. After the Dissolution the manor was sold in 1542 to Henry Clifford, earl of Cumberland, and the story runs on from there.
britannica-1911-bridgman-laura-dewey:
Laura Dewey Bridgman (1829–1889) was an American woman left blind and deaf in early childhood, whose schooling became a landmark case. Born on 21 December 1829 at Hanover, New Hampshire, the third daughter of a Baptist farmer, she was a frail baby prone to fits. At two years old a bad attack of scarlet fever destroyed her sight and hearing and blunted her sense of smell.

Her health slowly returned, but she stayed a blind deaf-mute, kindly treated at home and taken on country walks by a family friend, Asa Tenney. Word of her case reached Dr S. G. Howe, head of the Perkins Institution for the Blind at Boston, through men at Dartmouth College. He resolved to try teaching her, her parents agreed, and in October 1837 Laura entered the school, the start of the famed attempt the long entry follows.
britannica-1911-bromley:
Bromley is a borough in Kent, England, 10 and a half miles south-east by south of London by the South Eastern and Chatham railway, with 27,354 people in 1901. It lies on high ground north of the small river Ravensbourne in a well-wooded district, and has become a favoured home suburb for people whose business lies in London.

The former palace of the bishops of Rochester, built in 1777 over an older structure, anchors its past; the manor belonged to that see as early as Ethelbert's reign. In its gardens sits St Blaize's Well, a chalybeate spring held in high repute before the Reformation. St Peter and St Paul's church, mainly Perpendicular, keeps a Norman font and the gravestone of Dr Johnson's wife. Bromley College, founded by Bishop Warner in 1666 for twenty poor widows of loyal clergymen, now supports forty widows, with Sheppard College for their unmarried daughters beside it.
britannica-1911-buck-dudley:
Dudley Buck (1839–1909) was an American composer. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his career in music. He was born in Hartford, Connecticut, on 10 March 1839. His father was a merchant who backed his talent. Buck studied for four years in Europe. He trained at Leipzig, Dresden and Paris, from 1858 to 1862. He then came home to work as an organist.

Buck held organ posts at Hartford, Chicago and Boston. In 1875 he moved to New York. He helped Theodore Thomas conduct orchestral concerts there. From 1877 to 1903 he was organist at Holy Trinity church. His fame rests chiefly on church music. His cantatas include Columbus and The Golden Legend. The Light of Asia followed in 1885. He also wrote a grand opera, Serapis. His comic opera Deseret dates from 1880. He died on 6 October 1909.
britannica-1911-capuchin-monkey:
The capuchin monkey is a tropical American monkey. Its scientific name is Cebus capucinus. This 1911 Britannica article describes the genus. The plural name covers all the species of Cebus. Their range runs from Nicaragua down to Paraguay. Their native name is sapajou. They are typical members of the family Cebidae. Their tails can grip, but are shorter than their kin's.

The name capuchin comes from the hair on the crown. It thickens into a shape like a monk's cowl. The hair is not woolly, and the build is stout. These monkeys live in troops in the tall forest trees. They seldom, if ever, come down to the ground. They eat fruits, tender shoots and buds. Insects, eggs and young birds also form their diet. The article sets out their teeth, limbs and habits in turn. It places them among the prehensile-tailed monkeys of South America.
britannica-1911-cherry-valley:
Cherry Valley is a village of Otsego county, New York, in a township of the same name, 68 miles north-west of Albany. Its people numbered 792 in 1910, and the township counted 1,706 that year. The Delaware and Hudson railway serves the village. Farming and dairying shape the rich country around it, and a chair factory works there. Sulphur and lithia springs make it a summer resort.

A massacre during the War of Independence dominates the history given here. On 11 November 1778 Walter Butler and Joseph Brant attacked with 800 Indians and Tories. About 50 men, women and children were killed, most houses were sacked and burned, and more than 70 prisoners were carried off. Many prisoners died or were killed before they reached the Canadian settlements. Cherry Valley was incorporated in 1812.
britannica-1911-chertsey:
Chertsey is a market town in Surrey, England, 22 miles west-south-west of London, on the right bank of the Thames. Its urban district counted 12,762 people in 1901, and a bridge of seven arches, built in 1785, crosses the river. The parish church holds tablets to Charles James Fox and to Lawrence Tomson, a 17th century translator of the New Testament. The town centres a large residential district and trades in produce for London markets.

A great Benedictine abbey, founded in 666 as the first religious settlement in Surrey, once covered four acres here. Little remains beyond a traced plan, fish ponds and finds of carved stones, coffins and tiles. Abbot John de Rutherwyk rebuilt much of it between 1307 and 1346, and tenant anger at his copyhold changes led to rolls being burned in 1381. Fairs, markets, ferries and bridges fill the later history.
britannica-1911-chimney:
Chimney, in architecture, is that part of a building rising above the roof in which are the flues that carry smoke to the outer air. The word comes through French from a Latin term for an oven or furnace room. At first it covered the fireplace as well as the shaft. At Rochester Castle in 1130 the flue simply passed through the wall above the fireplace. Early shafts were round, held one flue and ended in a conical cap.

Only in the 15th century did smoke issue at the top, and later still did several flues share one shaft. Such shafts often stand in richly patterned brick, as at Hampton Court, the entry notes. French shafts at Meillant, Chambord and Blois carry carving and armorial devices. A second half treats factory chimneys, where height and heat set the draught. Round shafts in brick, iron, steel or concrete reach 180 to 200 feet.
britannica-1911-cibber-colley:
Cibber, Colley (1671–1757) was an English actor and dramatist, born in London on 6 November 1671, eldest son of the sculptor Caius Gabriel Cibber. At Grantham school he showed an early gift for verse, but a hoped-for place at Winchester was refused him. He went to London, served as a volunteer in the bloodless campaign of William of Orange, then joined Betterton's company at Drury Lane in 1690. Apprentice custom left him unpaid for three quarters of a year.

His comedy Love's Last Shift in 1696 and his Lord Foppington in Vanbrugh's Relapse fixed his stage fame, and later successes included The Careless Husband in 1704. With Wilks and Doggett he managed Drury Lane into its most prosperous years, and his Nonjuror of 1717 helped bring him the poet laureateship in 1730. In 1740 he published his Apology, an account of his life and of the stage of his time that Goldsmith and Johnson both praised.
britannica-1911-colombey: Colombey is a village of Lorraine. It stands four miles east of Metz. The brief hosted entry gives it one claim to notice. German and French forces fought a battle there on 14 August 1870. That fight is often called the battle of Borny. Borny is another village east of Metz. The entry names no commanders. It gives no course of the fighting. For the battle itself it points to two other entries. One covers Metz, and the other covers the Franco-German War.
britannica-1911-cooper-thomas-sidney:
Thomas Sidney Cooper (1803–1902) was an English painter born at Canterbury on 20 September 1803. Art drew him from his earliest childhood. His family's means barred any set training, though. Before he was twelve he worked in a coach painter's shop. Scene painting came next, and he swapped between the two trades for eight years.

All his spare hours still went to drawing and painting from nature. At twenty he went to London and drew in the British Museum. The Royal Academy took him as a student there. Back in Canterbury he lived as a drawing-master and sold sketches. In 1827 he settled in Brussels. Four years later he came back to London for good. His first Royal Academy picture in 1833 began a career of rare length. Farm scenes of East Kent fill his late list of works.
britannica-1911-cowley-charles-wellesley:
Henry Richard Charles Wellesley, first Earl Cowley (1804–1884), was a British diplomat. He was the eldest son of Henry Wellesley, first Baron Cowley. His mother was a daughter of the first Earl Cadogan. He thus stood as nephew to the duke of Wellington and to the marquess Wellesley. He was born on 17 June 1804 and entered the diplomatic service in 1824.

His first post of weight came in 1848. He became minister to the Swiss cantons in that year. That same year he went to Frankfort to watch the German parliament at work. A post as envoy to the new Germanic confederation followed, but held him for a short time only. In 1852 he was chosen to succeed Lord Normanby as ambassador in Paris. He held that great post for fifteen years in all. His Paris years, the entry holds, cannot be split from the joint history of England and France.
britannica-1911-darling-grace-horsley:
Grace Horsley Darling (1815-1842) was a British heroine born at Bamborough in Northumberland. Her father William kept the Longstone lighthouse on the Farne Islands. On the morning of the 7th of September 1838 the Forfarshire, bound from Hull to Dundee with sixty-three people aboard, struck the islands, and forty-three were drowned. From the lighthouse the wreck was seen, and father and daughter resolved to row out to it.

They knew that reaching the wreck was possible but returning would need the survivors' help, and they took the risk without pause. They brought back four men and a woman, then returned with two rescued men for the last four survivors. The Humane Society gave both its gold medal, and Grace died of consumption in 1842.
britannica-1911-fool-s-parsley:
Fool's parsley, in botany, is the popular name for Aethusa cynapium. It belongs to the family Umbelliferae and is a common weed in cultivated ground. The plant is an annual herb with a spindle-shaped root. Its stem is smooth, hollow and branched, standing one to two feet high. Its leaves are much divided and smooth, and it bears small compound umbels of small, irregular white flowers in summer.

The plant has a nauseous smell, the entry warns. Like other members of its order, such as hemlock and water-dropwort, it is poisonous. That warning is the point of the short notice: a common garden weed, much like true parsley in its divided leaves, can poison anyone who mistakes it for the herb. The entry gives the plant's family, form, height, flowers and danger in a few exact lines, and nothing more.
britannica-1911-fountains-abbey:
Fountains Abbey is one of the most celebrated church ruins in England. It lies in the sheltered valley of the river Skell, three miles south-west of Ripon in Yorkshire. The little Skell runs down clear and swift from Pateley Moor through a wooded valley. Ancient yew trees there may have sheltered the monks who first sought retreat on the spot. Steep rocky hills close the vale, and the ruins rise in an open glade, mainly on the stream's north side.

The church and the remains of domestic buildings let the abbey be rebuilt almost wholly in the mind. Its arrangements are typical of a Cistercian house. The article walks the reader through church, cloister and offices. The hosted file opens with the end of the Fountain article.
britannica-1911-frimley:
Frimley is an urban district in the Chertsey division of Surrey, England, 33 miles west-south-west of London by rail and a mile north of Farnborough. It held 8409 people in 1901. A healthy climate, a place in the sandy heath country of west Surrey, and nearness to Aldershot Camp have grown it into a residential township.

East of the town the moorland rises in the Chobham Ridges, and Bagshot village lies three miles north-east on its own heath. Bisley Camp, home since 1890 to the National Rifle Association meetings moved from Wimbledon, is four miles east. Conifers and rhododendrons suit the local soil, and large nurseries are given over to raising them. The entry is a brief gazetteer portrait of a fast-growing heath town.
britannica-1911-gilbert-sir-humphrey:
Sir Humphrey Gilbert was the Elizabethan seaman who planted the first English colony in North America. The hosted 1911 Britannica text preserves only the closing passage of his entry, covering his last voyage. It has him off Newfoundland on 30 July, choosing St John's as his centre on 3 August, and beginning the plantation on 5 August.

Sailing south with three vessels, he lost the largest near Cape Breton on 29 August. He then turned for England with the Golden Hind and the little Squirrel, refusing to leave the small frigate for the great ship. Off the Azores on 9 September the Squirrel went down with him, after his famous cry, reported by Captain Hayes, 'We are as near to heaven by sea as by land.' The entry's source list names Hakluyt and Gilbert's own Discourse of a Discovery for a New Passage to Cataia of 1576.
britannica-1911-hampden-sidney:
Hampden-Sidney is a village of Prince Edward county, Virginia. Richmond lies about 70 miles to the north-east. The village population is about 350. Daily stages link it to Farmville, the county-seat. Its fame rests on Hampden-Sidney College. The Hanover presbytery founded the school in 1776. Its first name was Hampden-Sidney Academy. The name honours John Hampden and Algernon Sidney.

Incorporation as a college came in 1783. James Madison and Patrick Henry were among the incorporators. Henry is believed to have drafted the charter. A theological school joined the college in 1812. It moved away to Richmond in 1898. In 1907–1908 the college had 125 students. Its library held 11,000 volumes. Its standard of instruction stayed high for generations. President William Henry Harrison was an alumnus. So were cabinet secretaries Bibb and Preston.
britannica-1911-hanley:
Hanley is a market town of Staffordshire, England. It lies in the Potteries district, 148 miles north-west of London. Its population in 1901 was 61,599. The parliamentary borough includes neighbouring Burslem. The town stands on high ground. Handsome municipal buildings and a free library serve it. A technical and art museum is also noted. Porcelain, tiles and earthenware are its manufactures.

Those trades employ most of the population. Women and children work in them almost as largely as men. Coal and iron are dug in the neighbourhood. Hanley is a modern development. Its municipal constitution dates only from 1857. The county borough followed in 1888. Etruria, adjoining, began with Wedgwood's pottery works of 1769. Under the Potteries federation scheme Hanley joined Stoke-on-Trent in 1910.
britannica-1911-havergal-frances-ridley:
Frances Ridley Havergal (1836–1879) was an English hymn-writer. She was born at Astley, Worcestershire, on 14 December 1836. Her father was the Rev. William Henry Havergal. At seven she began writing verse. Most of that verse was religious in character. As a hymn-writer she proved particularly successful. Modern English church collections include several of her hymns.

Her collected Poetical Works appeared in 1884, after her death. She died at Caswell Bay, Swansea, on 3 June 1879. She was only forty-two years old. Her sister wrote the Memorials published in 1880. The entry is a very short notice. It gives her dates, her clerical family and her hymn-writing fame. Nothing in it reaches beyond those few facts.
britannica-1911-hill-daniel-harvey:
Daniel Harvey Hill (1821–1889) was an American Confederate soldier, born in York district, South Carolina, in 1821. He graduated at the Military Academy in 1842 and was breveted for bravery in the Mexican War. In 1849 he resigned to teach mathematics, ending as head of the North Carolina Military Institute at Charlotte in 1859.

In 1861 Hill became a colonel and won the action of Big Bethel. As a major-general he led a division at Fair Oaks and in the Seven Days, and his stand at South Mountain let Lee concentrate for Antietam. In 1863 he went west and led a corps under Bragg at Chickamauga. He surrendered with Johnston in April 1865. His magazine The Land We Love (1866–1869) had great influence in the South.
britannica-1911-hody-humphrey:
Humphrey Hody (1659–1707) was an English divine, born at Odcombe in Somersetshire. He entered Wadham College, Oxford, in 1676 and became a fellow in 1685. In 1684 he published a Latin dissertation against the letter of Aristeas. It showed that the letter, source of the famous account of how the Septuagint was made, was a late forgery by a Hellenist Jew.

The dissertation was held conclusive, though Isaac Vossius answered it with anger. Hody wrote the Prolegomena to the chronicle of John Malalas (1691), and served as chaplain to Bishop Stillingfleet and then to Archbishops Tillotson and Tenison. In 1698 he became regius professor of Greek at Oxford, and in 1704 archdeacon of Oxford. His History of English Councils and Convocations appeared in 1701. His four-volume De Bibliorum textis originalibus (1703) reworked the Septuagint study and replied to Vossius. He died in January 1707.
britannica-1911-keighley:
Keighley is a municipal borough in the West Riding of Yorkshire, England, 17 miles west northwest of Leeds, on branches of two railways. Its people numbered 41,564 in 1901. It stands in a deep valley near the meeting of the Worth with the Aire, and a canal between Liverpool and Hull gives it water carriage to both coasts.

The chief buildings are the parish church of St Andrew, first raised in the time of Henry I and rebuilt in 1878, and the Gothic mechanics' institute and technical school of 1870. A grammar school founded in 1713 has grown to count a trade school for boys and a grammar school for girls. The chief industries are the making of woollen goods, spinning, and the making of sewing and washing machines and tools. The town was made a borough in 1882.
calvary-alley:
Alice Hegan Rice wrote a novel of a poor lane, dated 1917. Mrs. Wiggs of the Cabbage Patch heads her past work on the title page. Walter Biggs drew the plates. A small band of Kentucky writers, her road mates in letters, get the book. Thirty-one chapters line the frame in view.

A fight opens the tale. The Snawdors at home and the Clarkes at home set the two poles. Youth court and a term on trust come next. Butternut Lane, a house loss, and stirred aims fill the early run. The state steps in at the heart. Work hours eight to six, slack time, and Miss Bobinet fill the mid-run. Dan, a signal tower, and Calvary Cathedral mark the late turns. Mac, two fires at once, and fate's hand close the heads. Lane pride and law's hand form the stakes.
cappy-ricks-or-the-subjugation-of-matt-p:
Cappy Ricks, or the Subjugation of Matt Peasley, by Peter B Kyne, is a sea story about a lumber shipping magnate and the skipper who defies him. Kyne dedicates the book to the ideal American sailor and shipowner through his own friends. Among them stands Captain Ralph E Peasley of Maine, who sailed the first five masted schooner ever built through a record typhoon and up the Yang Tse under his own hand.

Chapter I calls Cappy master of many ships and skipper of none, which states the whole feud. Retired to the office, Cappy rules his fleet by cable and temper, while Matt Peasley, the man from blue water, commands at sea under the Blue Star flag. Bad news from Cape Town starts the quarrel of wills. Kyne writes shipping as a contest between shore authority and a captain's judgment.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on abbey defines a monastery canonically erected and autonomous, with at least twelve religious. Monks live under an abbot, nuns under an abbess. An autonomous priory is ruled instead by a prior. That distinction was unknown in monasticism's first centuries, when England's twelve great cathedral priories stood under priors with the diocesan as abbot.

Other priories began as cells or offshoots of great abbeys, remaining dependent on the parent house. The parent abbot appointed the prior and could remove him at will. Originally monastery meant the dwelling of a solitary or a community alike, while words like cenobium and congregatio marked community houses alone. Monasteries took names from place, founder, or a monk whose life shed lustre on them, and later from a saint whose relics they kept.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-corv: The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Corvey, also called New Corbie, describes a Benedictine monastery in Westphalia, founded about 820 from Corbie in Picardy by Emperor Louis the Pious and St. Adelhard. Its abbots held princely rank in the empire, its school cultivated arts and sciences, and it preserved the first five books of Tacitus' Annals. Missionaries from Corvey, chiefly St. Ansgar, evangelised northern Europe, and Widukind wrote his Saxon history there. The school faded after the fifteenth century, and the abbey was secularised in 1803.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-achor-valley:
Achor Valley is the scene of the death of Achan, the troubler with whom its name is linked. Osee foretells this gloomy, ill-omened valley becoming an opening of hope for the returning exiles of Israel. Another prophet pictures the same glorious future, with herds lying down there, as Isaiah 65:10 records.

The valley lay along Juda's north boundary, past Jericho toward the Jordan. Modern scholars identify it with Wady-el-Kelt, usually written Akor. The short entry thus moves from judgment to promise, giving a place of death a second meaning as a sign of restoration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anne-hanson-d:
Anne Hanson Dorsey, a novelist, was born at Georgetown in 1815 and died at Washington in 1896. Her father was Navy chaplain William McKenney, her mother Chloe McKenney. In 1837 she married Lorenzo Dorsey, and in 1840 she converted to the Catholic faith. For more than half a century she gave her talent to Catholic fiction, pioneering light Catholic literature and writing for the young. Her deeply religious stories brim with living interest and world knowledge.

Her only son was killed serving in the Union Army during the Civil War, and she left three daughters. Pope Leo XIII twice sent his benediction, and Notre Dame gave the Laetare medal. Her chief works include The Student of Blenheim Forest, Guy, the Leper, Tears of the Diadem, Woodreve Manor, and Conscience. Others are Oriental Pearl, The Flemings, and Nora Brady's Vow. Mona, the Vestal, The Old Gray Rosary, Tangled Paths, Adrift, and The Palms follow.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anthony-champ:
Anthony Champney, a controversialist, was born in England about 1569 and died there about 1643. He studied at Reims in 1590 and at Rome in 1593. As a priest he was imprisoned at Wisbech, worked against the Jesuits, and acted for the Appellant Clergy in Rome in 1602. He became president of the English College of Arras, a doctor of theology and Fellow of the Sorbonne. Douai College had him as vice-president from 1619 to 1625 and from 1628 until his return to England.

His books include An Answer to a Letter of a Jesuited Gentleman (1601). A Manual of Controversies followed in 1614, and A Treatise of the Vocation of Bishops in 1616. His Defence of the Appendix to the Antidote predates 1624. Also: Mr. Pilkington his Parallela Disparalled (1620) and An Answer to Featley's Fisher catched in his own Net (1623). His History of Queen Elizabeth is in manuscript, once in the Old Chapter archives but in the Westminster Archives since 1879.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anthony-rey:
Born at Lyons in 1807, Anthony Rey died near Ceralvo, Mexico, in 1847, an educator and Mexican War chaplain. Schooled at Fribourg's Jesuit college, he entered the novitiate in 1827 and taught at Fribourg and Sion. The United States received him in 1840 as philosophy professor at Georgetown College; in 1843 he moved to Saint Joseph's in Philadelphia. By 1845 he was the Maryland provincial's assistant, Trinity Church pastor, and college vice-president.

In 1846 he was appointed a United States Army chaplain, ministering to the wounded and dying at the siege of Monterey amid great dangers. After the city fell, he stayed at Monterey and preached to the rancheros. Against United States officers' advice, he set out for Matamoras, preaching to Americans and Mexicans at Ceralvo. A band under Canales apparently killed him, and his body, pierced with lances, was found days later. Letters of his dating from November 1846 were printed in the Woodstock Letters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aubrey-beards:
Aubrey Beardsley was an English artist born at Brighton in 1872 who died at Mentone in 1898, aged twenty-five. The entry paints him as a precocious boy who never quite grew up. Full of merriment and mischief, his wish to shock narrow opinion shaped much of his early work. After a clerkship, he trained in illustration, won praise from Burne-Jones and Puvis de Chavannes, and at nineteen took on the huge task of illustrating the Morte D'Arthur.

A Studio article in 1893 made his work sought after. In 1894 he became art editor of the Yellow Book, later starting the Savoy with Arthur Symons. His finest illustrations include Salome, The Rape of the Lock, and Volpone, marked by vigor, invention, and a dainty, sure line. Bad health dogged him from boyhood, and a man of deep feeling throughout, he became a Catholic near the end of his life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aulne-abbey:
Aulne Abbey, also called Alna, was a former Cistercian monastery near Landelies on the Sambre, in the Diocese of Liege. It began as a Benedictine house founded by St Landelinus about 656. Before 974 the Benedictines gave way to secular clerics living in common, who took the Rule of St Augustine in 1144. Three years later, at the urging of Bishop Henry de Leyen of Liege, Cistercian monks from Clairvaux took over, with Franco de Morvaux as first Cistercian abbot.

From then it flourished as a Cistercian house until the French burned it at the end of the eighteenth century. The fire came only a short time after the abbey had been rebuilt on a larger scale. Its library, holding forty thousand books and five thousand manuscripts, was destroyed with it. The entry cites three histories of the house, by Boulmont, Cloquet, and Lebrocquy, for its origins, splendors, trials, and ruins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bangor-abbey:
Bangor Abbey names two famous monastic houses, one in Ireland and one in England. The Irish abbey stood in County Down on Belfast Lough's southern shore. Its name, Beannchor, comes from beann, a horn, after cattle horns scattered there by a Leinster king. It was also called the Vale of Angels, where St Patrick was said to see the valley filled with angels.

St Comgall, born in Antrim in 517, founded the abbey in 559 after friends drew him from a lonely island retreat. His rigid rule of unceasing prayer and fasting attracted crowds, and Bangor grew into Ulster's greatest monastic school. Within its rampart, monks studied Scripture, theology, logic, geometry, arithmetic, music, and the pagan classics. When Comgall died in 601, three thousand monks looked to Bangor's abbot for guidance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-barent-van-or:
Barent van Orley, or Bernard, was a painter born at Brussels about 1491, who died there in 1542. He studied under Raphael in 1509, then returned to Brussels and painted an altarpiece for Furnes's Holy Cross confraternity in 1515. In 1518 he became official painter to Margaret of Austria, Regent of the Netherlands. Two years later he entertained Dürer, who painted his portrait, now in the Dresden Museum.

After Margaret's death in 1530, Mary of Hungary renewed his official appointment. Though Catholic, he attended Lutheran meetings in his father's house and, with his brother, paid fines and did public penance at St Gudule. He painted in oil and tempera, designed fine glass windows for St Gudule, and supervised Vatican tapestries from Raphael's cartoons with Michael Cocxie. Tapestries from his own drawings hang at Hampton Court, the Louvre, and Caserta, and his pictures glow from grounds of gold leaf.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bath-abbey:
Bath Abbey began as a nunnery founded by King Osric in 676, later becoming a Benedictine monastery reformed by St Dunstan. King Edgar was crowned in its St Peter's church in 973. Its abbot St Elphege, later Archbishop of Canterbury, was killed by Danes in 1012. In 1088 William Rufus gave the abbey to John de Villula of Wells, and its head became a cathedral prior, not an abbot.

A 1137 fire wrecked the city and abbey, which were promptly rebuilt, and in 1245 Innocent IV settled Bath-Wells election disputes by alternating the election city. Prior Hollewell surrendered the house to Henry VIII in 1539, ending monastic life, its revenues valued at £617. The present St Peter's, begun about 1500 and finished in 1572, is a late Perpendicular specimen, and English Benedictines have served Bath's Catholic mission since 1679.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-battle-abbey:
Battle Abbey was founded by William the Conqueror on the Hastings battlefield of 1066, seven miles from Hastings town. Begun the next year on a great scale, it was finished only under William Rufus, for 140 monks though never more than sixty lived there. Its first monks came from Marmoutier in Normandy, and it was consecrated on 11 February 1094 to the Trinity, St Mary, and St Martin.

William offered his father's sword and coronation robes there, and the abbey won sanctuary, treasure trove, and exemption from bishops and secular courts. Its mitred abbot sat in Parliament and could pardon any criminal met on the way to execution. The high altar stood where Harold fell, and its Roll of Norman companions grew with unauthentic additions over time. At suppression in May 1538, seventeen monks remained; a Catholic church and priest serve Battle today.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-beaulieu-abbe:
Beaulieu Abbey, Latin Bellus Locus, was a Cistercian house in Hampshire, one of three monasteries founded by King John about 1204. Thirty monks from Cîteaux peopled it, and John's endowment included New Forest land, corn, money, 120 cows, twelve bulls, a golden chalice, and a yearly tun of wine. Its buildings were dedicated in 1246 before Henry III, his queen, and Richard of Cornwall.

Innocent III made it an exempt abbey with sanctuary rights, sought by Ann Neville in 1471 and by Perkin Warbeck in 1497. Shortly before suppression in 1539, thirty-two sanctuary men lived within its precincts with their families. Granted to Thomas Wriothesley in 1536, it passed to the Dukes of Buccleuch, whose nephew now owns the restored gatehouse. No stone remains of its 335-foot church, though its foundations were traced and marked in sand.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-belley:
Belley is a diocesan entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia, covering a French see whose land matches the department of Ain. Suppressed under the Concordat, it was restored in 1822, drawing districts from the archdioceses of Lyons and Chambéry. Local tradition credits second-century martyrs with first bringing the faith there.

Bishops form the spine of the entry, from Vincentius, named in 552, through medieval saints such as Anthelm, a Carthusian leader. Later sections list religious houses, schools, and the diocese's present shape. The piece blends legend, early records, and nineteenth-century rebuilding into one compact local history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-boyle-abbey:
Boyle Abbey, a Cistercian house on the River Boyle nine miles from Elphin, was founded by Maurice O'Duffy in 1161 as a daughter of Mellifont. Its church was consecrated in 1218, and many of its abbots became bishops in Connaught, above all at Elphin and Achonry. Princes of Connaught, especially the MacDermots of Moylurg, retired there before death.

English troops under Fitzgerald and McWilliam seized the abbey in 1235, stripping monks of goods, vessels, and habits in their own cloister. Elizabeth suppressed it, and its lands passed to Patrick Cusack in 1569, revealing one of Ireland's richest endowments. Leases later went to William Ussher and Sir John King. Its abbot Donchad O'Daly, dead in 1250, was praised as the Ovid of Ireland. The abbey now lies in ruins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-buckfast-abbe:
Buckfast Abbey, a Devon monastery two miles from Ashburton in the Dart valley, predates the Norman Conquest, though its founding date is unknown. The best authorities place it in the mid-tenth century, and its earliest sure document is Canute's grant of Zeal Monachorum between 1015 and 1035. Early in the twelfth century it joined Savigny's Benedictine congregation, and in 1148 its thirty houses passed with Savigny to Clairvaux and the Cistercians.

Buckfast grew into a leading house of the Exeter diocese, starting the district's famed woollen trade, backing other crafts, and keeping strict discipline and fervor. Discipline slackened in the fourteenth century and numbers fell, yet learning and local love held until the dissolution. Gabriel Donne, intruded after John Rede's death about 1535, surrendered the house in 1538. Benedictines regained the ruin in 1882, and Mass and Office sounded there again on 29 October 1882.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-walme:
An entry on Charles Walmesley, an English Benedictine bishop who was also an astronomer and mathematician. Born in 1722, the fifth son of John Walmesley of Wigan, he was educated at Douai, professed as a Benedictine at Paris in 1739, and took his doctorate at the Sorbonne. The British government consulted him on calendar reform, and he joined the Royal Society of London as a fellow, and the academies of Paris, Berlin, and Bologna.

Walmesley became coadjutor to Bishop York in 1756 and ruled the Western District from 1770. During the No Popery riots of 1780, a mob burned the new Catholic chapel at Bath and his presbytery, destroying registers, archives, and his library. In 1789 he led the bishops in condemning the Catholic Committee's new oath as unlawful. His General History of the Christian Church, issued under a pen name, ran through many editions in Britain and America. He died at Bath in 1797.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cistercian-ab:
Waverley in Surrey, near Farnham, was founded on 24 November 1124 by William Gifford, Bishop of Winchester. It was the second daughter of L'Aumone in Normandy and the first Cistercian monastery in England. Furness was founded a few years earlier, but it belonged to Savigny until 1147, so Waverley's Cistercian priority stands. Bishop William endowed it richly, and Henry de Blois confirmed and increased its privileges.

The first century was Waverley's golden age: it founded six monasteries and still counted seventy choir religious and a hundred and twenty lay brothers in 1190. Floods in 1201 forced a move to higher ground, and the new church opened in 1231. Henry the Third visited in 1225 and asked for honorary membership. By its suppression under Henry the Eighth in 1536 only thirteen religious remained, and today nothing but the bare site survives.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cornelius-hee:
Thomas Meehan's entry treats Cornelius Heeney, merchant and philanthropist. Born in King's County, Ireland, in 1754, he died at Brooklyn in 1848. After a mercantile education in Dublin, he emigrated to America in 1784, working with the Astor family's founder in a New York fur store. Their employer left the business to John Jacob Astor and Heeney.

Heeney continued in the same line, amassing a considerable fortune. A bachelor, he spent his income on religious and charitable works. Saint Peter's, Saint Patrick's, and New York's Catholic Orphan Asylum received generous gifts. One of New York's first Catholic office-holders, he served five State Assembly terms from 1818 to 1822. There he kept giving, planning to devote his whole estate to charity. An 1845 act incorporated it as the Trustees and Associates of the Brooklyn Benevolent Society, for the poor and orphans. Its income ran about $25,000, and by 1909 it had given over a million dollars.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dahomey:
A mission entry describes the Dahomey Vicariate Apostolic in West Africa, matching the French colony of the same name. Stretching north from a 75-mile Slave Coast shoreline to the French Sudan, it covers about 59,000 square miles, with under half a million people in 1902. Palm kernels and palm oil were its chief exports, and its people were chiefly Fon of the Ewe family.

Three native dynasties ruled until one conquered the others about 1728 and set up a despotism, tempered only by fetishism, until France captured and exiled King Behanzin in 1892. The Faith came first in 1660 with Franciscans, met murder and opposition, and revived only in 1860. By the time of writing the mission counted 8,900 Catholics, 32 priests, and schools for over 1,800 pupils.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-denis-mary-br:
A life of Denis Mary Bradley, first Bishop of Manchester, New Hampshire, born in 1846 at Castle-island in Kerry and dead at Manchester in 1903. Brought to America at eight after his father's death, he studied at Holy Cross College and Saint Joseph's Seminary at Troy, where he was ordained in 1871. Portland and cathedral posts followed, then the pastorate of Saint Joseph's at Manchester in 1881.

When the new see was raised in 1884, Saint Joseph's became his cathedral and he its first bishop. Scattered rural Catholics drew his first care, and he held the diocese's first synod in 1886. Zeal and warmth built up Catholic life across the state, and at his death even non-Catholic pulpits in Manchester praised the loss to city and state.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dermond-o-hur:
A life of Dermond O'Hurley, Archbishop of Cashel, who died in June 1584. Schooled on the Continent and a doctor of both laws, he taught at Louvain and Reims before Rome named him archbishop in 1581, consecrating him before he had taken priesthood. Landing in Ireland in 1583, he sought shelter with the Earl of Ormonde but was betrayed to Dublin Castle.

His captors, hoping for evidence against Kildare and Delvin, won leave to torture him, and Walsingham advised roasting his feet in boots of oil and salt over fire. He cried out for mercy from Jesus, son of David, yet refused every offer to abandon his faith. At dawn he was hanged in secret near Saint Stephen's Green, and friends buried him at Saint Kevin's churchyard.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dominique-jea:
Dominique-Jean Larrey, Baron Larrey, was a French military surgeon born at Baudean in July 1766. His parents were so poor that only the village priest's kindness schooled him. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how, after his father's death, the boy of thirteen was sent to his uncle, a successful surgeon of Toulouse. At twenty-one he went to Paris, passed a brilliant contest into the navy, and later studied under Dessault.

Joining the army in 1792, he founded the flying ambulance the next year, a corps of surgeons and nurses who reached the wounded on the field. His surgical memoirs of the campaigns in Russia, Germany, and France were printed at Philadelphia in 1832. He died at Lyons in 1842, a father of battlefield surgery.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-downside-abbe:
Downside Abbey, near Bath in Somerset, began at Douai in Flanders in 1605 under Saint Gregory the Great. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how the Venerable John Roberts, first prior, gathered English monks vowed in the Spanish Benedictine congregation. In 1611 the Abbot of Saint Vaast at Arras built them a monastery at Douai and is honored as founder. Attacks from outside and quarrels over union with other English Benedictines troubled the early years.

Pope Urban the Eighth settled the disputes by the bull Plantata in 1633. From the start a school for sons of English Catholic gentry formed part of the house, run on English public school lines. The entry follows the community to its English home, with guides, necrologies, and sketches of old Downside to close.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dryburgh-abbe:
Dryburgh Abbey is a monastery of the Premonstratensian canons, also called Norbertines or White Canons, four miles southeast of Melrose in Scotland. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how Hugo de Morville, Constable of Scotland, founded it about 1150 with a community from Alnwick. The site is a wooded promontory ringed on three sides by the River Tweed, and the church was given to the Blessed Virgin.

Edward the Second burned the house in 1322 while retreating from Scotland, but Robert the First restored it with generous gifts. At the Dissolution it became a temporal lordship granted by James the Sixth to the Earl of Mar. Today visitors seek chiefly the tomb of Sir Walter Scott in Saint Mary's Aisle, where his wife and eldest son also lie.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-worsle:
Edward Worsley was an English Jesuit writer born in Lancashire in 1605 and dead at Antwerp in 1676. He is said to have studied at Oxford, though his name is missing from the university registers, and it is not certain that he took Anglican orders. He became a Jesuit in 1626 and studied at Liege, where he later taught philosophy, logic, and Scripture with a high name for learning.

Made a professed father in 1641, he worked for a time in London, then served as rector of the Liege college from 1658 to 1662 and as procurator at Antwerp. Most of his books answered Stillingfleet, among them Truth Will Out in 1665, Protestancy Without Principles in 1668, Reason and Religion in 1672, and a work on infallibility in 1674. Anti-Goliath came out after his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ellwangen-abb:
Ellwangen Abbey was the earliest Benedictine monastery in Wurtemberg, in the diocese of Augsburg some thirty miles north-east of Stuttgart. Hariolfus, Bishop of Langres, founded it about 764, though a few authorities say as early as 732. It became a royal abbey. The privilege is said to have come from Henry II in 1011. Charles IV confirmed it in 1347. Its superior sat among the princes in the Diet by 1500.

Benedictine life there ended in the first half of the fifteenth century, and in 1460 the house became a college of secular canons under a provost. Its famous men include Abbots Lindolf and Erfinan, praised by Mabillon as authors. Ermenrich wrote a life of Saint Solus. Adalbero became Bishop of Augsburg in 894. Later abbots rose to Mainz and Augsburg, and by the eighteenth century the canons held a wide estate of manors. Most of the old buildings still stand, now in state hands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-erdington-abb:
Erdington Abbey, in a suburb of Birmingham, Warwickshire, belongs to the Benedictine congregation of Saint Martin of Beuron, Germany, and is dedicated to Saint Thomas of Canterbury. Driven from Germany by the Falk laws, four exiled monks went to Erdington at the request of Bishop Ullathorne and the Reverend Daniel Haigh. Haigh, a convert Anglican clergyman, gave them the splendid Gothic church he had built from his own private fortune, as a thank-offering for the gift of the true Faith.

Father Haigh's modest presbytery was the first monastery. There Dom Placid Walter, Dom Hildebrand de Hempstine, Dom Leo Linse, Dom Leodgar Stocker, and a lay brother took up their abode in October 1876. Two years later Dom Hildebrand succeeded him and built a monastery large enough to chant the Divine Office in choir. It was finished in 1880, when the monks numbered eleven with three lay brothers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eugene-o-grow:
Eugene O'Growney was an Irish priest and scholar who gave his short life to the Irish language. Born at Ballyfallon in County Meath in 1863, he first learned of Ireland's own tongue at Saint Finian's seminary in Navan. At Maynooth he studied Irish, antiquities, and history, was ordained in 1888, and became professor of Irish in 1891. He also edited the Gaelic Journal.

In 1893 he helped found the Gaelic League in Dublin and served as its vice-president until his death. His Simple Lessons in Irish, first printed in the Weekly Freeman, taught thousands the language of their forebears. Failing health took him to Arizona and California in 1894. He died at Los Angeles in 1899, and his body was later brought home for burial at Maynooth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-evesham-abbey:
Evesham Abbey was a great Benedictine house in Worcestershire, founded about 701 by Saint Egwin, third Bishop of Worcester, and dedicated to the Blessed Virgin. His charter of 714 tells how his herdsman Eoves saw Our Lady, and Egwin, visiting the spot, saw her too and was told to build a monastery there. Kings Ethelred and Kenred of Mercia helped the work. Egwin is said to have resigned his see to become first abbot, ruling until his death in 717, and his shrine grew rich and famed for miracles.

Under the Normans the abbey grew into one of England's largest. Its church ran near three hundred feet. It held two dependent cells and patronage of seventeen parishes. Its abbots sat in the House of Lords, and exemption from the bishops of Worcester was confirmed at Rome in 1206. In 1539 his successor surrendered the house to Henry VIII, and its buildings were soon quarried.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-faversham-abb:
Faversham Abbey was a Cluniac Benedictine house in Kent, about nine miles west of Canterbury. King Stephen and Queen Matilda founded it about 1147. Thirteen monks from Bermondsey, led by Prior Clarimbald, formed the community. Stephen, Matilda, and their son Eustace were buried in its great church.

Later kings confirmed the abbey's grants, and its abbots sat in Parliament. Townsfolk complained of the abbey's tolls on markets, brewing, and swine pannage. The last abbot signed the Act of Supremacy in 1534. Surrendered in 1538, the abbey now survives only in outer wall fragments.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-folkestone-ab:
Folkestone Abbey, more rightly Folkestone Priory, stands in east Kent, thirty-seven miles from Maidstone. St. Eanswith, daughter of King Eadbald of Kent, founded a nunnery there in 630, dedicated to St. Peter. Danes destroyed it, and in 1095 Nigel de Mundeville raised a monks' house on the same site. The new house was an alien priory, a cell of the Norman abbey of Lonley, honouring Mary and Eanswith.

Sea erosion forced a move in 1137 to the site of the present Folkestone church. Made denizen and free of Normandy, it escaped the fate of most alien priories under Henry V. It lasted to the dissolution and was surrendered on 15 November 1535, worth about £50 yearly. Only a Norman doorway survives, though foundations can be traced for a good distance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fort-augustus:
St. Benedict's Abbey at Fort Augustus in Inverness-shire was, when this entry was written, the only Benedictine monastery for monks in Scotland. John, third Marquess of Bute, pushed the project in 1874, hoping to restore monastic life to a land that had lost its abbeys at the Reformation. Dom Jerome Vaughan raised about seventy thousand pounds for the building. The site, a dismantled fort of 1729 given by Lord Lovat, took its name from the Duke of Cumberland.

Monastic buildings rose between 1876 and 1880 around a quadrangle, and in 1882 Pope Leo XIII made the house an independent abbey under the Holy See. A boys' school ran for about sixteen years but closed in 1894. By the early twentieth century the community numbered about fifty monks and lay brothers, with a library of some twenty thousand volumes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fountains-abb:
Fountains Abbey was a Cistercian monastery on the river Skell about two and a half miles from Ripon in Yorkshire. It began in 1132 when thirteen Benedictine monks of St. Mary's Abbey, York, led by Prior Richard, left to seek a stricter discipline, obtained land from Archbishop Thurston, and put themselves under St. Bernard, who sent Geoffrey of Clairvaux to instruct them in Cistercian rule.

Early buildings were burned in 1146 by followers of Archbishop William of York, but new building soon produced the great church whose ruins still stand, finished before 1250. Daughter houses included Sawley, Roche, Woburn, Meaux, Kirkstall, and Vandy, with a colony sent to Bergen in Norway. At the Dissolution in 1540 Abbot Marmaduke Bradley surrendered the abbey, then home to thirty-one monks, and its ruins remain carefully preserved.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-frederick-apt:
Frederick Apthorp Paley, a classical scholar born near York in 1815, built a vast output of Greek and Latin editions after his Cambridge career broke down. Grandson of William Paley of the Evidences, he studied at Shrewsbury and St. John's College, Cambridge, but was expelled from residence in 1846 on suspicion of steering a pupil toward Rome. He entered the Catholic Church that same year.

For fourteen years he lived as a private tutor and by his pen, then returned to Cambridge when the tests eased, and later taught at the short-lived Catholic University College at Kensington. His editions of Aeschylus, Euripides, Homer, and a dozen others ran to more than fifty volumes and filled school and college needs of the day, though later scholarship soon passed them by.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-frederick-oak:
Frederick Oakeley, youngest son of Sir Charles Oakeley, moved from Oxford high churchmanship into the Catholic Church alongside Newman. Born at Shrewsbury in 1802, he graduated from Christ Church in 1824 and became a fellow of Balliol. He took the Margaret Chapel living in 1839 and stood by Ward at his condemnation in 1845. After defending Tract XC, his bishop suspended him.

Oakeley then retired to Newman's community at Littlemore and followed him into the Catholic Church within weeks. Ordained in 1847, he spent thirty-three years as a canon of Westminster and rector at Islington. Small, lame, and short-sighted, he still swayed many by his writing and talk. His books range from sermons and ethics to notes on the Tractarian movement.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-furness-abbey:
Furness Abbey, five miles from Ulverston in north Lancashire, grew from a small Savigny colony into a rich Cistercian house. Monks sent from Savigny settled at Tulketh in 1124, then moved in 1127 to Stephen of Boulogne's gift of Furness forest, with woods, fisheries, mills, salt works, and mines. Growth ran so fast that Calder went out as a daughter house in 1134.

By 1148 the whole Savigny family, Furness included, had joined the Cistercians under Saint Bernard. Furness later ruled four Irish monasteries and, through Rushin, touched the Isle of Man, where its monks became bishops. Thirty-two abbots are known, the last Roger Pyle. In April 1537 abbot, prior, and twenty-eight monks signed the surrender, and the grand ruins still stand.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-j-wigl:
George J. Wigley, an architect turned Paris journalist, helped plant the Society of Saint Vincent de Paul in England. One of the laymen around Frederick Ozanam at the Society's founding, he wrote letters to The Tablet at Ozanam's suggestion describing its aims and work. The editor Lucas took up the cause in print, and in January 1844 the English branch formed, with Wigley, then in London, among its original thirteen members.

About 1860 Wigley led in forming the Peterspence Association in England and France to aid the Holy Father, and Pius IX soon gave him the Cross of Saint Gregory the Great. He died in Rome in January 1866 while nursing a Protestant English sailor, one of his Vincent de Paul cases. He brought the man into the Church on his deathbed, then caught the same disease and died in the Brothers of Saint John of God hospital.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-glastonbury-a:
Glastonbury Abbey is a Benedictine monastery in Somersetshire, England, pre-eminently the centre of early Christian tradition in England. Once an island ringed by broad fens, with Glastonbury Tor rising about four hundred feet above them, it formed a natural sanctuary. A Catholic Encyclopedia article warns that legend and fact are now so mingled that no power can sift truth from falsehood with certainty.

Tradition says Joseph of Arimathea and eleven companions built a wattled church to the Virgin in the year 63. Saint Patrick later became abbot and taught the hermits to live as cenobites. Dunstan, educated in its cloister, ruled it as abbot until his elevation to the episcopate. After the Norman Conquest it prospered, but in 1539 it was the last religious house standing in Somerset when royal commissioners arrived, and its end came with Henry VIII.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-harney:
Two American brothers share this entry: William Selby Harney, soldier and convert, and John Milton Harney, poet and Dominican. William, born near Haysboro, Tennessee, in 1800, joined the army in 1818 and fought in the Black Hawk, Florida, and Mexican wars. He commanded in the Sioux troubles of 1855 and befriended the missionary De Smet, whose help made peace.

His seizure of San Juan Island in 1858 set off the Oregon boundary dispute with Britain. In the Civil War he was briefly held by Confederates while heading the Department of the West, retiring a brevet major-general in 1863. John, born in 1789, studied medicine, served in the navy off South America, edited a paper, entered the Catholic Church, and joined the Kentucky Dominicans, and died in their ranks in 1825.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-foley:
Henry Foley, born at Astley in Worcestershire in 1811, trained as a solicitor and practised in Worcester before the Oxford Movement led him to embrace the Catholic faith in 1846. Five years later, after his wife's death, he sought admission to the Society of Jesus as a lay brother. Against advice to prepare for the priesthood, he insisted that it was Our Lady's wish that he remain a lay brother. For thirty years he served as lay brother socius to the English provincial.

In that post Foley produced his vast life's work, The Records of the English Province of the Society of Jesus, eight volumes of original research and historical detail assembled with rare perseverance. The account ranks him with Father Henry More as historian of the Society, and notes his companion volume Jesuits in Conflict on the sufferings of English Jesuit confessors. He died at Manresa House, Roehampton, in 1891.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-holy-cross-ab:
Holy Cross Abbey stands in picturesque ruins on the Suir's right bank, some three miles south-west of Thurles in County Tipperary. Not the largest among Ireland's Cistercian houses, it led them all in beauty of architectural detail, with fine proportions and delicate stone carving. Donald O'Brien, king of Thomond, founded it in 1169.

It was the eleventh of forty-two Irish houses founded before the Reformation by followers of St. Bernard. Its fame came from a shrine of the Holy Cross, one of the greatest relics in Christendom, which drew pilgrims as a leading shrine for more than three and a half centuries. The cruciform church still shows the pillared shrine where the relic was exposed for public veneration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-holyrood-abbe:
Holyrood Abbey stood in Edinburgh, founded in 1128 by King David I, probably for Augustinian canons brought from St. Andrews. Tradition says David founded it in thanks for a miraculous escape from a hart's horns while hunting near Edinburgh on Holy Cross day. Its church kept Scotland's Black Rood, a piece of the True Cross that David's mother, Margaret, had brought.

English hands took the relic at Neville's Cross in 1346, set it in Durham Cathedral, and there it vanished when the Reformation came. The first abbot was Alwyn, the king's confessor, who resigned about 1150. Robert, James V's natural son, was the twenty-ninth and final Catholic abbot. He went over to Protestantism in 1559, married, and swapped his abbacy for Orkney's temporalities.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-curley:
James Curley, an astronomer, was born at Athleague in County Roscommon, Ireland, on 26 October 1796 and died at Georgetown in the District of Columbia on 24 July 1889. His early schooling was scant, though a teacher from his home town spotted and built up his gift for mathematics. He left Ireland while young, landing at Philadelphia on 10 October 1817, where he worked two years as a bookkeeper before teaching mathematics at Frederick, Maryland.

In 1826 he entered Washington's old seminary to train for the priesthood, teaching one of its classes at the same time; that seminary, founded in 1820, shut the following year. He then joined the Society of Jesus on 29 September 1827, taught again at Frederick after his novitiate, and in 1831 was sent to Georgetown College to teach natural philosophy. He studied theology as well and took priestly orders.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-rooseve:
James Roosevelt Bayley served as the first bishop of Newark, New Jersey, and as the eighth archbishop of Baltimore, Maryland. He was born at Rye, New York, on 23 August 1814 and died at Newark on 3 October 1877. His Dutch and English ancestors, who were not Catholic, stood out locally. His father was the son of Dr Richard Bayley, anatomy professor at Columbia College and founder of New York's quarantine system. Mother Seton, foundress of America's Sisters of Charity, was his aunt.

He took his name from his maternal grandfather, the merchant James Roosevelt, who made him his heir. Roosevelt altered his will after Bayley became a Catholic priest, wrongly supposing that priests could hold no property. A large share of the money went to raising New York's Roosevelt Hospital. Bayley spent his school days at Amherst College, where he once dreamed of going to sea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-shirley:
Poet and dramatist James Shirley was born in London on 18 September 1596. He died there in October 1666. As a boy he attended Merchant Taylors School from October 1608 to June 1612. He matriculated at St John's College, Oxford, in 1612. There he won the esteem of Laud, the college president. In 1617 he took his B.A. at St Catharine's Hall, Cambridge.

Soon after taking orders in the English Church in 1619, he served as curate near St Albans. He stayed there until his conversion to Catholicism. After conversion he taught for a living and became master of St Albans' Edward VI School. When that school failed, he moved to Gray's Inn, London, in 1625 to set up as a playwright, as he put it. His praise of Benedictines in The Grateful Servant shows intimacy with monks of that order. His first poem, Eccho, opened a long stage career.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-sebast:
Johann Sebastian von Drey was a theologian who helped found the Catholic faculty at Tubingen and its long-running journal. Born in 1777 to very poor parents, he was spotted by his parish priest, schooled at Ellwangen on charity and tutoring, and ordained in 1801. Years of private study in Kant, Fichte, and Schelling gave his later writing its philosophical cast.

He taught at Rottweil and then at the new Catholic university of Ellwangen, where he lectured on dogmatics, the history of dogma, apologetics, and introduction to theology. When Ellwangen merged into Tubingen in 1817, Drey joined its staff and in 1819 founded the Theologische Quartalschrift with his colleagues, writing many essays and reviews for it. His early Latin dissertations on Justin Martyr and on confession drew notice, one of them even a report to Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-casey:
John Casey was an Irish mathematician who rose from village schoolteacher to Fellow of the Royal Society. Born at Kilkenny in 1820, he taught under the Board of National Education, becoming head master of Kilkenny's Central Model School, while studying mathematics, Latin, French, and German in his leisure. Solving Poncelet's problem by geometry brought him to the notice of Trinity College men.

Entering Trinity in 1858 near his fortieth year, he won a sizarship, a scholarship, and his degree in 1862, then taught mathematics at Kingstown School, training candidates for the Indian Civil Service. In 1873 he became professor at the Catholic University in Dublin, refusing a Trinity professorship to advance Catholic higher education. He edited a mathematics journal, corresponded widely, and won honors from the Royal Irish Academy, the London Mathematical Society, and the Royal Society before his death in 1891.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-francis-:
John Francis Bentley was the English architect of Westminster Cathedral, the most striking church building raised in England since the Reformation. Born at Doncaster in 1839, he showed an early bent for architecture despite his parents' doubts. He apprenticed himself at sixteen to the clerk of works at Loversall Church. He trained in Manchester and London and set up on his own in 1868.

A firm believer in medieval principles, he gave personal attention to every detail from foundation to furniture. He excelled as draughtsman and colorist in marble, metal, stained glass, and heraldry. Commissions included Manning's seminary at Hammersmith, St. Anne's Cathedral at Leeds, and St. Mary's in Chelsea. In 1894 he began Westminster Cathedral after studying Italian basilicas and Ravenna mosaics, devoting himself to it until his death in 1902.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kearney:
Kearney is a Nebraska diocese carved from the western half of Omaha by Pope Pius X on 8 March 1912. This entry records its creation, its first bishop, James Albert Duffy, appointed 25 January 1913, and its place as a suffragan, or subordinate diocese, of Dubuque.

Spread over 38,000 square miles of western Nebraska, it counted about 15,200 Catholics, 58 churches, 21 parishes, 35 missions, and 34 stations without churches. The entry names the counties it covers, from Keyapaha and Cherry in the north to Scotts Bluffs and Kimball in the west. Schools and care work feature too: one academy, three parish schools with over 680 pupils, Sisters of St. Francis schools at Ashton and Alliance, and a hospital at Alliance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kimberley:
Kimberley is a vicariate apostolic in north-west Western Australia, raised by Leo XIII on 5 May 1887 as a suffragan of Adelaide and run by the Bishop of Geraldton. The district, one of six land districts in the state, holds plentiful gold.

Bishop Matthew Gibney of Perth sailed out in person on 4 June 1890 with Trappist Abbot Ambrose to found a settlement for the local Aboriginal people. Their station, the Holy House of the Sacred Heart at Beagle Bay, housed some five to six hundred people in a bark monastery and bark church. After the Trappists left for Europe, Pallottine Fathers took over, with flourishing stations at Broome and Disaster Bay, and a solid monastery and convent rose in 1903.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lorsch-abbey:
Lorsch Abbey, in Hesse ten miles east of Worms, was one of the most famed monasteries of the old Frankish-German empire. Count Cancor and his widowed mother Williswinda founded it in 764, and Chrodegang of Metz dedicated it to St. Peter and became its first abbot.

Relics of St. Nazarius, won from Pope Paul I, arrived in 765 and drew pilgrims from across Europe, with miracles reported at the shrine. Gifts of land and towns raised Lorsch to a principality, rich and powerful, and a nursery of learning. That same wealth and sway pulled it into feuds and wars, and after forty-six Benedictine abbots its glory faded toward ruin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maelbrighte-o:
Maelbrighte O'Hussey, Irish Maol Brighde ua Heodhusa, Latin Brigidus Hossaeus, also Giolla-Brigid and Bonaventura Hussey, was a Franciscan friar born in the diocese of Clogher, Ulster. His life is obscure until 1 November 1607, when he joined the original Irish Franciscans at St. Anthony's college, Louvain, after time at Douai.

At Louvain he lectured in philosophy, then theology, and won fame for deep knowledge of Irish history and language, esteemed even in his own day. His works, all in Irish, include A Christian Catechism of 1608, the first book printed on the Continent in Irish character. It was often reprinted, beside a metrical abridgement in 240 verses, poems on heresy and entering the order, and a letter to Father Nugent. He stayed guardian at Louvain until his death in 1614.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-malling-abbey:
Malling Abbey was a house of Benedictine nuns at West Malling in Kent. Domesday Book mentions the nunnery in 1080. Its church lands had fallen to Bishop Odo of Bayeux at the Conquest. Archbishop Lanfranc made him restore them in 1076. Gundulf, made Bishop of Rochester the next year, built the abbey.

Its founding date is doubtful, given as early as 1078 and as late as 1106. In token of subjection to Rochester, it paid ten pounds of wax and one boar each year. Fire in 1190 destroyed abbey and village, but both soon rose again. At the dissolution, Abbess Dame Vernon and eleven nuns signed the surrender, and the house passed to Cranmer. Little of the first building stands, save a Norman tower, church fragments, and the refectory. Private owners held it until 1893, when an Anglican community founded by Father Ignatius bought it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mark-aloysius:
Mark Aloysius Tierney was an English priest and antiquarian, born at Brighton in 1795 and dead at Arundel in 1862. Schooled by Franciscans at Baddesley Green, he entered St Edmund's College, Old Hall, in 1810 and was ordained there in 1818. 

Ill health moved him to the country mission of Slindon in Sussex. In 1824 he took up Arundel chaplaincy to the Duke of Norfolk, spending his life there in historical and antiquarian study. His chief aim was a new edition of Dodd's Church History of England, with documents gathered by himself and Kirk. Volume one appeared in 1839, but volume five in 1843 halted the work, as reviving seventeenth-century secular-regular disputes offended readers. He won fellowship of the Society of Antiquaries in 1833 and the Royal Society in 1841. He served as Sussex Archaeological Society secretary, and after the hierarchy's restoration became first canon penitentiary of Southwark.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mary-aloysia-:
Mary Aloysia Hardey, of the Society of the Sacred Heart, established all her order's convents up to 1883 in the eastern United States, Canada, and Cuba. She was born at Piscataway, Maryland, in 1809 and died at Paris in 1886. Her parents came from old Maryland Catholic families, and after her father moved to Louisiana she became an early Sacred Heart pupil at Grand Coteau in 1822.

She entered the order in 1820 and became superioress of St Michael in 1835. Ten voyages to Europe, five to Cuba, and constant travel as provincial and visitatrix taxed her greatly, yet her chief care was forming fervent religious as consecrated teachers, not merely raising convents. Named assistant general in 1871, she lived at Paris's mother-house, visited America in 1874, 1878, and 1882, and was buried at Kenwood, Albany, in 1900.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mathew-carey:
Mathew Carey was an author and publisher, born at Dublin, Ireland, in 1760 and dead at Philadelphia in 1839. He was the first prominent Catholic in America's publishing trade and issued in 1790 the first Douay Bible printed in America. His father was a baker of small fortune. 

At fifteen he disappointed his father by choosing bookselling and printing, apprenticing at once. An omnivorous reader, he built knowledge by persistent study. His first article, in the Hibernian Journal in 1777, attacked duelling, prompted by a friend's duel. In 1810, though a Democrat, he backed re-chartering the first United States Bank. Boyhood reading for Ireland's cause moved him to write on Irish wrongs, and from 1819 he wrote on the tariff. Married in 1791 in straitened means, he later grew rich yet frugal, fathering nine children including economist Henry C. Carey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-montreuil-abb:
Montreuil Abbey was a former house of Cistercian nuns in the Diocese of Laon, now Soissons. It was founded in 1136 by Bishop Bartholomew of Laon and soon numbered nearly three hundred sisters.
