Early members wove and embroidered, tilled fields, cleared forest and weeded soil. The crowd grew unwieldy, and Clairvaux barred new novices until numbers fell to one hundred.

Wars in the seventeenth century drove the nuns to the hospital of Saint-Lazare near the city. The Revolution suppressed the house. Through the Middle Ages Montreuil drew pilgrims for its Sainte Face, the Veil of Saint Veronica. That picture was a copy of the Vera Effigies in Saint Peter's at Rome. Jacques Pantaleon, later Urban IV, gave it in 1249 to his sister the abbess.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-new-abbey:
New Abbey, the Abbey of Sweetheart, named New Abbey Pow to distinguish it from Dundrennan in the same county, stands near the River Pow in Kirkcudbrightshire, Scotland, about eight miles from Dumfries. Its foundress was Lady Devorgilla, daughter of Alan, Lord of Galloway. She built the monastery to hold an ivory and silver casket embalming her husband John de Baliol's heart, giving the abbey its sweetheart title.

Sweetheart is the last Cistercian abbey in Scotland in order, begun in 1275 as a daughter of Dundrennan, of the Clairvaux lineage. Henry, its first abbot, built a magnificent early English church, 203 feet long, with a central tower 92 feet high, nave with aisles, transepts with eastern chapels, and an aisleless choir. Monastic buildings in proportion stood within a massive granite wall, eight to ten feet high, large portions of which remain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-new-jersey:
New Jersey, one of the original thirteen American states, ratified the Federal Constitution on 18 December 1787, preceded only by Delaware and Pennsylvania. Its capital is Trenton. It stretches 160 miles north to south and 70 east to west, covering 7,815 square miles, bounded by New York, the Hudson and Atlantic, Delaware Bay, and the Delaware River. Its 1910 population was 2,537,167.

Despite large mountainous and forest areas, it is more densely populated than the most fertile prairie states or the great manufacturing states. It holds, for its area, more railway miles than any other state. Its farms yield a larger income per cultivated area than the richest Mississippi valley states, and it ranks sixth in manufactures. The entry covers its four natural belts, towns, schools, and the Catholic Church's dioceses, parishes and institutions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patrick-rober:
Patrick Robert Guiney was a Boston lawyer and soldier born at Parkstown in County Tipperary on 15 January 1835 and dead at Boston on 21 March 1877. His father, of Jacobite blood with one French strain, carried the boy, not yet six, to New Brunswick on a second voyage after a runaway marriage. The family settled at Portland, Maine, where Guiney attended public schools, then entered Holy Cross College but left before graduating on a point of honour.

After his bookish father's death he read law under Judge Walton and was admitted at Lewiston in 1856, showing early genius for criminal law. A Republican, he won the Massachusetts animal-protection society's first suit. In 1859 he married Janet Margaret Doyle in Boston's old cathedral. Home life and rising practice broke on the Civil War. There he served with distinction, rose to command of his regiment and brigade, and was gravely wounded at the Wilderness in 1864.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-gallwey:
Peter Gallwey was one of Victorian London's best-known priests, born at Killarney in 1820. Schooled at Stonyhurst, he joined the Jesuits at Hodder in 1836, was ordained in 1852, and professed his final vows two years later. As prefect of studies at Stonyhurst he improved the course of study, then in 1857 moved to the Jesuit church in London, where he spent nearly all his remaining life.

Deep spirituality, preaching, retreat-giving, and love of the poor made him widely venerated. Energy and enterprise marked everything he touched, and several London convents and Catholic institutions owed their founding and growth largely to his zeal. His books include Salvage from the Wreck, funeral sermons of 1890, and Watchers of the Passion, meditations drawn from his retreats. He died in London in 1906.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ramsey-abbey:
Ramsey Abbey, in Huntingdonshire, England, was founded by Ailwine, a Saxon noble, in 969. This encyclopedia entry tells that Saint Oswald of York encouraged the undertaking. He advised that where men renounce the world, the air grows wholesome and earth's fruits abound. Famines and plagues vanish, the state is well governed, prisons open, and captives go free. The shipwrecked find relief, the sick are healed, and the weak gain means of recovery.

The chosen site, Ramsey, then the largest island of an Ouse marsh, took its name from the ram's island. Monks later joined it to the mainland by a causeway they built. Aednoth, nephew of Ailwine and commissioned by Oswald to prepare the ground, built a wooden church there. As soon as all stood ready, the community began its life, and the chronicle of Ramsey Abbey, Dugdale's Monasticon, and Wise's history of its rise and fall supply the entry's sources.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reading-abbey:
Reading Abbey, in Berkshire, England, was founded by Henry the First in 1121. This encyclopedia entry quotes William of Malmesbury, who describes it as built between the Kennet and the Thames. The spot suited travellers bound for England's most populous cities. There Henry placed monks of the Cluniac Order, who remain, Malmesbury writes, a model of holiness and tireless, delightful hospitality.

The foundation charter says the new house takes the place of three monasteries: Reading, Choisey and Leominster. It dedicates the abbey to the Blessed Virgin and Saint John the Evangelist. It grants it every civil privilege of royal monasteries, and bids the abbot spend his alms on entertaining prior, pilgrims and guests. Hugues de Boves, late Prior of Saint Pancras at Lewes, served as first abbot, and relics included the skull of Saint Philip, given by King John.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-langl:
Richard Langley was a Yorkshire landowner who gave his house and fortune to sheltering Catholic priests under Elizabeth I. Living mostly at Ousethorpe in the East Riding, he married, raised a son and four daughters, and turned his home into a refuge. He even built a hidden underground retreat where priests could hide from searchers.

Betrayal ended that quiet work in the autumn of 1586. Soldiers searched his houses at Grimthorpe and Ousethorpe, found two priests in hiding, and seized Langley himself. Hauled before the President of the North, he refused the oath of the queen's supremacy over the church. A first jury was dismissed for fear it would acquit him. A second condemned him without proof that he knew the men he sheltered were seminary priests. He was hanged, drawn, and quartered at York on 1 December 1586.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-shell:
Richard Shelley was an English Catholic gentleman who died a confessor in the Marshalsea prison in London in the winter of 1585-86. The third son of a Sussex landowner, he spent time abroad attending his uncle, the last Grand Prior of England of the Knights of St John. Allowed to return home in May 1583, he later presented a petition on behalf of persecuted fellow Catholics.

Two surviving accounts of that petition disagree, one saying it went to the queen and the other to Parliament, and they differ on dates as well. The one certain result was Shelley's committal to the Marshalsea on 15 March 1585. He was still alive there in October 1585, sick when his servant came to him, and died shortly after, steadfast in his faith. The entry warns readers not to confuse him with a namesake Richard Shelley of Findon, who was also imprisoned for religion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-roger-brooke-:
Roger Brooke Taney, pronounced Tawney, was the fifth Chief Justice of the United States. Born in Calvert County, Maryland, in 1777 to Catholic parents, he was schooled privately and by tutors until fifteen, then entered Dickinson College at Carlisle and graduated in 1795. In 1796 he went to Annapolis to read law with Jeremiah Townley Chase. Admitted to the bar early in 1799, he practised in Calvert County and was elected to the House of Delegates, its youngest member.

Moving to Frederick in 1801, he lost re-election there. In 1806 he married Anne Phoebe Charlton Key, sister of Francis Scott Key, later author of the Star-Spangled Banner. He helped win acquittal for General Wilkinson at his 1811 court martial. Elected to the state senate in 1816, he defended a Methodist minister charged with inciting slaves in 1819. At Baltimore from 1823 he became a leading lawyer, Maryland's attorney-general in 1827, and United States attorney-general under Jackson in 1831.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rufford-abbey:
Rufford Abbey was a Cistercian monastery by the Rainworth Water, a couple of miles south of Ollerton in Nottinghamshire. Gilbert de Gant founded it in or about 1147, settling monks from Rievaulx Abbey there. He endowed it with the manor of Rufford, soon adding Wellow, Barton, and Willoughby.

Later gifts made the abbey rich enough to supply victuals for Edward II's Scottish expedition in 1310. It contributed to York's losses in 1319, yet in 1409 escaped a king's tenth for extreme poverty. The last abbot but one, Rowland Blyton, left in 1533 for Rievaulx. His successor Thomas Doncaster took a pension at the 1536 dissolution, soon becoming rector of Rotherham. The abbey passed in 1537 to George Talbot, Earl of Shrewsbury, and later to the Savile family.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-john-of:
John of Beverley, bishop of Hexham and afterwards of York, was born at Harpham in Yorkshire and died at Beverley on 7 May 721. As a boy he studied under Archbishop Theodore at Canterbury, who is said to have given him the name John. He joined the Benedictine order and spent time at Hilda's monastery at Whitby. He won fame as a preacher and expounder of Scripture and was consecrated bishop of Hexham on 25 August 687.

He had lived in retreat at Erneshowe across the Tyne and returned there for seclusion, especially in Lent. Present at the synod on the Nidd in 705 for Wilfrid's case, he was moved to York that year after eighteen years at Hexham. Diligent in visitation and kind to the poor, he trained pupils including Bede. After buying Inderawood, later Beverley, he founded and endowed a monastery there and retired to it, resigning York to his pupil Wilfrid.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sherborne-abb:
Sherborne Abbey in Dorsetshire, England, was founded in 998 on a site that had been the seat of the Bishop of Western Wessex since Saint Aldhelm in 705. The Benedictine Rule came in under Bishop Wulfsy III, who also governed the monastery as abbot, with the monks forming his chapter. Roger of Caen separated the offices in 1122, when the see moved to Sarum and the abbey church lost cathedral rank.

Bishop Roger replaced the small Saxon church of Saint Aldhelm with a larger Norman one, later rebuilt until it stands almost entirely in perpendicular style. A Lady chapel came in the thirteenth century, and Abbot John Brunyng began a great restoration in 1415, carried on by William Bradford. Quarrels with parishioners, a great fire in 1437, and the Dissolution close the story. The fan vaulting of the choir survives, and the entry calls it unrivaled.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sir-patrick-a:
Patrick Alphonsus Buckley, soldier, lawyer, statesman, and judge, was born near Castletownsend, County Cork, in 1841 and died at Lower Hutt, New Zealand, on 18 May 1896. He was schooled at Cork's Mansion House School, Saint Colman's College in Paris, the Irish College in Paris, and Louvain's Catholic University. When Piedmont invaded the Papal States in 1860, he led Irish Papal Brigade recruits from Ostend to Vienna. He served under General Lamoricière and was taken prisoner at Ancona.

After the war he returned to Ireland, then emigrated to Queensland, finished his legal studies, and was admitted to the Bar. Called to the Legislative Council in 1878, he served as Colonial Secretary and Upper House leader in the Stout-Vogel ministry of 1884 to 1887. Then as Attorney-General and Colonial Secretary under Ballance from 1891 to 1895, when he became a Supreme Court judge.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-fursey:
Fursey, abbot of Lagny near Paris, carried Irish monastic fire from Lough Corrib to East Anglia and Francia. Son of Fintan of South Munster and Gelgesia of Hy-Briuin, he was baptized by Brendan the Traveller, his father's uncle, and educated by Brendan's monks. Under Abbot Meldan, his soul-friend, he embraced religious life, and legend credits his prayers with raising a chieftain's twin children. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 16 January, about 650.

He founded a monastery at Rathmat on Lough Corrib, drawing crowds, then sought relatives for the house in Munster. His wanderings would take him to Burgh Castle in Suffolk and finally to Lagny, with his brothers Foillan and Ultan following his path. The entry opens a career of foundations, visions, and crossings that made an Irish abbot a father of Frankish monasticism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-john-viann:
John Vianney, curé of Ars, overcame weak Latin and conscription to become France's beloved parish priest. Born at Dardilly near Lyons on 8 May 1786 to Matthieu Vianney and Marie Beluze, he was sent in 1806 to the curé Balley at Ecully. Balley had opened a school for church students. Of average intelligence, with knowledge limited to a little arithmetic, history, and geography, he found learning, above all Latin, excessively hard. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Ars to 4 August 1859.

Matthias Loras, later first bishop of Dubuque, helped him with Latin. Then conscription struck: war with Spain led Napoleon to withdraw church students' exemption in Cardinal Fesch's diocese. Matthieu failed to buy a substitute, so his son had to go. His regiment soon received marching orders, and on departure morning Jean-Baptiste went missing in the manner the entry recounts. From that unpromising start grew the curé of Ars.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stanbrook-abb:
Stanbrook Abbey, a house of Benedictine nuns between Malvern and Worcester, descends from an exile foundation at Cambrai. Dedicated to Our Lady of Consolation, it bore the title of the original foundation in Spanish Flanders in 1625. Monks of the English Congregation effected it, and the community always remained under their jurisdiction.

Of the nine English ladies who began it, Helen More, Dame Gertrude, was chief foundress through her father Cresacre More's liberality. Cresacre was great-grandson of Thomas More, giving the community special claims on that martyr's patronage. The other foundresses included Margaret Vavasour, Anne Morgan, and Catherine Gascoigne. Dame Frances Gawen, lent by Brussels Benedictines to train postulants, ruled as abbess for a time. Catherine Gascoigne, abbess from 1629 to 1676, then succeeded from the community's own body.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stephen-brink:
Stephen Brinkley, confessor of the faith, ran a secret Catholic press under Elizabeth and vanished after torture. Born about 1550, he belonged to a Catholic association of unmarried men of property, organised by George Gilbert and blessed by Gregory XIII in 1580. Its members lived on bare necessaries, spent the rest for the Church, raised funds for priests, and arranged introductions to guard priests and laity against betrayal.

When Parsons and Campion prepared a vigorous press propaganda, Brinkley managed their secret press with help from Marian priests and one Brooks. From Greenstreet house at East Ham in Essex came devotional and controversial works that defied the regime. Arrested, imprisoned, and tortured, he was lost to view after 1585. The entry recovers a layman who risked everything for the printed word.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sydney:
Sydney became an archdiocese on 15 February 1842, after starting as the Vicariate Apostolic of New Holland in 1834. Its first vicar, the Benedictine John Bede Polding, was consecrated in London in June 1834. On his Roman visit of 1841 to 1842, he prompted the creation of Hobart and Adelaide, with Melbourne and Brisbane detached later. Six New South Wales sees now serve as its suffragans.

When Polding landed, only four priests served the district, and the 1833 census counted 17,283 Catholics among 60,794 colonists. Government aid told a stark tale. Catholics got 4,000 dollars, against 95,355 for the Church of England, apart from its lands. Ten Catholic schools shared about 2,000 dollars. By 1910 the archdiocese taught 25,000 pupils, ran eight hospitals, and kept seven orphanages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tavistock-abb:
Tavistock Abbey stood on the Tavy River in Devonshire, England. Earl Ordgar founded it for Benedictines in 961, and his son Ordulf completed it in 981. King Ethelred confirmed its charter that year. Endowed with lands in Devon, Dorset, and Cornwall, it grew into one of the west's richest monasteries. Its church honoured Our Lady and St Rumon, an early Irish saint of Cornwall.

Danes burned the church in 997, but Abbot Livingus rebuilt it splendidly. Livingus and his successor Aldred both became bishops of Worcester, and Aldred is said to have crowned William the Conqueror. Abbot John Dynynton won the mitre in 1458, and Richard Banham became a lord of Parliament in 1513. Twenty-five years later the last abbot surrendered the house, and its revenues stood at £902. Only the refectory, two gateways, and a porch survive.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-abbey-of-:
The Abbey of Athelney, in Somerset, England, was founded by King Alfred in 888 as a Benedictine house. Athelney was then a small island amid morasses in East Ling parish. It held two acres of land, covered with alders and wild animals, reachable by boat. Here Alfred sheltered from the Danes and built the abbey to the Saviour, Peter, Paul, and Egelwine. He staffed it with monks, under John of Saxony as abbot.

The church was four piers bearing the main fabric with four chancels. Little is known of the abbey from the eleventh century to the dissolution, except Glastonbury's attempts to annex it. It was not rich. An indulgence of thirty days came in 1321 for rebuilding help, and the monks begged Edward I to remit an unpayable corrod. The last abbot, Robert Hamlyn, surrendered with eight monks in 1540, receiving £50 a year and his Long Sutton prebend, with revenues of £209.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-bailey:
Thomas Bailey, a controversialist who died about 1657, began as an Anglican clergyman and ended as a Catholic royalist in exile. The son of the Bishop of Bangor, he studied at Magdalen College, Cambridge, became sub-dean of Wells, and took a doctorate at Oxford during the Civil Wars. Service in the king's retinue after Naseby and travel abroad with Catholic help led him to convert.

Back in England he published a defence of episcopacy that angered Cromwell's government and landed him in Newgate prison, where he wrote Herba Parietis, or The Wall-flower, on his captivity. Freed, he retired to Italy and served in Cardinal Ottoboni's household at Ferrara. He also published a life of John Fisher, though its core text was Richard Hall's.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-cardin:
Thomas Wolsey, cardinal and Archbishop of York, rose from an Ipswich family of substance to become Henry VIII's chief minister. Born about 1471, he took his Oxford degree at fifteen, became a fellow of Magdalen, and was ordained priest in 1498. Talent for administration carried him from chaplaincies to the court of Henry VII, and then to Henry VIII, whom he served as diplomat and councillor.

Wolsey built a European policy of shifting alliances, playing Francis I of France against the Emperor Charles V while pressing for a general peace and a crusade against the Turks. He also founded colleges at Ipswich and Oxford, though the king later moved to suppress them. His fall came with the king's divorce case, and he died at Leicester Abbey in 1530 on his way to face treason charges.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-chisho:
Thomas Chisholm Anstey, lawyer and politician, was born in London in 1816, the son of one of the first settlers in Tasmania. Educated at Wellington and University College, London, he became one of the earliest converts of the Oxford movement and taught law at Prior Park College near Bath. He soon gave up teaching for politics, joining O'Connell's forces as a champion of Catholics in England and Ireland.

Elected to Parliament for Youghal in 1847, he opposed Palmerston's foreign policy and pressed for repeal of the Irish and Scottish unions. After leaving Parliament in 1852 he became Attorney General of Hong Kong in 1854, but clashed with Governor Bowring and was suspended in 1858. He practised law at Bombay until his death there in 1873.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-hussey:
Thomas Hussey, Bishop of Waterford and Lismore, was born in County Meath in 1746 and died at Tramore in 1803. Sent to the Irish College at Salamanca, he joined the Trappists, but the pope asked him to take orders, and he rose at the court of Spain in Madrid. About 1767 he became chaplain to the Spanish embassy in London, where Johnson, Burke and other leading men counted him among the ablest informed men of the day.

When war broke out between England and America, Hussey handled Spanish affairs in London and dealt directly with George III and Pitt. His mission to detach Spain from the American cause failed. A fellow of the Royal Society from 1792, he later championed the Catholic cause in Ireland and pressed its case at Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thorney-abbey:
Thorney Abbey, in Cambridgeshire, takes its name from the isle of thorns where Saxon hermits lived for some three centuries. In 972 Ethelwold, Bishop of Winchester, refounded it for Benedictine monks with King Edgar's help. He brought the body of St. Botulph and other Saxon saints there, and the church, first dedicated to Christ and his Mother, became known as St. Mary and St. Botulph's.

After the Norman Conquest a new church 290 feet long replaced Ethelwold's building and was finished in 1108. Charters of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries show a rich house, valued in Domesday Book as highly as Peterborough. William of Malmesbury called it an image of Paradise. Its last abbot, Robert Blyth, surrendered it to Henry VIII in 1539, and the Norman nave still serves as the parish church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tintern-abbey:
Tintern Abbey, in Monmouthshire on the Welsh border, was founded in 1131 by Walter de Clare for Cistercian monks from Aumone in France. His son Gilbert, first Earl of Pembroke, and probably his grandson Richard Strongbow, conqueror of Ireland, were buried there. The great church dates from the end of the thirteenth century, and rich gifts flowed in from the founder's family and other noble houses.

The last abbot, Richard Wych, reported a net income under two hundred pounds a year in 1535, with thirteen monks in residence. The abbey was suppressed in 1536 under the act dissolving smaller houses, and the king granted it in 1537 to the Earl of Worcester. Its roofless church, 245 feet long on the banks of the Wye, still ranks among the most beautiful ruins in England.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-anne-mari:
Anne Marie Javouhey founded the Sisters of St Joseph of Cluny, born at Chamblanc in the Diocese of Dijon on 11 November 1779, who died on 15 July 1851. Her congregation began by easing the miseries left by the Revolution, and in 1819 its scope widened to foreign missions. In 1822 Mother Javouhey herself opened a house at Gorée in West Africa.

After two years in Senegal and nearby lands she moved to the British colony of St Mary's in Gambia, giving herself wholly to victims of a raging pestilence. Back in Senegal she won French government help for a plan to educate Africans in Europe and send them home as missionaries. Meagre results followed, largely from the toll of disease, yet the entry follows her founding work across three continents.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-george-be:
George Beesley, also spelled Bisley, was a martyr born at The Hill in Goosnargh parish, Lancaster, of an ancient Catholic family, who died on 2 July 1591. Ordained priest at the English College at Reims on 14 March 1587, he left for England on 1 November 1588. Young, strong, and robust, and a man of singular courage, he was captured by Topcliffe late in 1590 and tortured until reduced to a skeleton.

He bore all with invincible courage and could not be made to betray his fellow Catholics. He suffered under the statute of 27 Elizabeth, merely for being a priest, in Fleet Street, London. His last words were Absit mihi gloriari nisi in Cruce Domini Nostri Jesu Christi, and after a pause, Good people, I beseech God to send all felicity. The entry gives a brief, vivid life of a steadfast priest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-john-buck:
John Buckley, alias John Jones and John Griffith, in religion Godfrey Maurice, was a priest and martyr of Wales who died on 12 July 1598. The entry warns at once that his history is much confused with that of Robert Buckley, the Westminster monk who alone linked pre- and post-Reformation English Benedictines. That confusion explains seeming discrepancies in John's story.

Claims that he was a Shropshire native or that he was jailed in the Marshalsea in 1582 to 1584 are incorrect, the entry states. John came of a good Welsh family that had stayed faithful to the church. The account follows his Franciscan life, his mission work, and his execution, separating as far as possible the martyr's true record from his namesake's.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-john-hamb:
John Hambley was an English martyr who suffered in 1587, born and schooled in Cornwall, converted by reading one of Father Persons's books in 1582. After his course at Reims from 1583 to 1585, he returned and worked a year in the western counties. Betrayed and seized about Easter 1586, he was tried and condemned at Taunton.

He kept his life for the moment by denying his faith, then broke prison and fled to Salisbury. The next August, however, the Protestant bishop there, hating the old faith, ordered Catholic houses searched on the Assumption's eve, hoping to catch a priest, and Hambley was recaptured. Now in worse plight than ever, his fears grew, and he again offered conformity, this time giving up the names of most of his Catholic friends. Tried again the next Easter, he suffered.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-sir-thoma:
Sir Thomas Dingley was the prior, or head, of the Knights of St. John of Jerusalem in England when Henry VIII moved against the order. A bill of attainder, a law that condemned a person without a trial, declared him guilty of high treason in April 1539. He was beheaded on Tower Hill that July, beside Sir Adrian Fortescue.

The charge said Dingley had urged foreign rulers to wage war on the king, yet no proof was ever produced against him. The same attainder swept up other victims, among them Margaret Pole, Countess of Salisbury. Old chroniclers even disagree on his death date, giving 9 or 10 July. The entry closes at Clerkenwell, where the gateway tower and crypt of the order's great priory church still stand.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-william-h:
William Hartley was a Derbyshire martyr executed at Tyburn in October 1588. Born about 1557, he entered St John's College, Oxford, at eighteen and became a chaplain there, but was expelled in 1579 and went to Reims, where he was ordained at Châlons. Returning to England in 1580, he helped Fathers Persons and Campion by printing and distributing their books.

Arrested in August 1581, he was held in Marshalsea Prison, laid in irons for saying Mass in a cell, indicted for treason but not tried, then sent into exile in 1585. After recovering his health at Reims and making a pilgrimage to Rome, he returned to his perilous mission. Seized again in Holborn in September 1588, he was suspected, unjustly, of having lapsed. At Tyburn he won great credit for constancy, meek, modest, and grave in bearing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-venerable-joh:
John Bodey was a scholar and martyr executed at Andover in November 1583. Born at Wells in 1549, he studied at Winchester and New College, Oxford, where he became a fellow in 1568. Deprived with seven other fellows by the Protestant visitor in 1576, he went to Douai to study civil law, returned to England in 1578, and probably married.

Arrested in 1580 and kept in iron shackles at Winchester, he was condemned with schoolmaster John Slade for upholding the old religion and denying the royal supremacy. Doubts about the sentence led to a second trial at Andover on the same charge. From prison he wrote that iron borne for this cause would outshine gold and precious stones in heaven. At his death he kissed the halter, calling it the sweetest chain ever about a man's neck, and protested that he had committed no treason.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-venerable-ral:
Ralph Ashley was a Jesuit lay brother executed at Worcester in April 1606. First heard of as cook at Douai College, he left for Valladolid in 1590, entered the Society there, and returned to England because of ill health. Captured by Dutch heretics on his journey, he showed, in Father Tesimond's praise, great courage, and landed in England in March 1598 to serve Father Edward Oldcorne.

Eight years on, both men were seized at Hindlip, near Worcester, and committed to the Tower with Father Garnet and lay brother Nicholas Owen. The two servants were terribly tortured; Owen died of his torments, while Ashley's trembling signatures on his surviving confessions testify to his constancy. Remanded with Oldcorne to Worcester, they were tried, condemned, and executed together, giving, in the entry's words, an admirable example of heroically faithful service.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-waltham-abbey:
Waltham Abbey, formally Waltham Holy Cross, stood in Essex some ten miles northeast of London on the Middlesex border. On Tofig's death his property lapsed to the Crown, and Edward the Confessor granted the estate to Harold, who enlarged the church and founded a college of secular canons.

Dedicated to the Holy Cross in 1060 by Archbishop Cynesige of York, with Wlwin as first dean, it is said, though disputed, that Harold's body was brought there for burial after Hastings. Henry II replaced the secular canons with Augustinian Canons in 1177, Walter de Gant became first abbot seven years later. Waltham grew into the country's most important Augustinian house, its mitred abbot sitting in Parliament, exempt from episcopal visitation, and favoured by Rome and Crown. At the dissolution in 1537 it was valued at over £1,079 a year, the richest religious house in Essex, outlasting every other abbey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wearmouth-abb:
Wearmouth Abbey was a Benedictine monastery on the River Wear in Durham, St Benedict Biscop founded it in 674 on ground granted by Egfrid, King of Northumbria, and dedicated to St Peter. Ten years later Biscop founded its sister house at Jarrow on the Tyne in honour of St Paul. The two, six or seven miles apart, are so linked in early history that they are often spoken of as one.

Biscop brought French workmen to build his church in Roman fashion and furnished it with glass windows, previously unknown in England, pictures. Flourishing under Biscop and successors Easterwin and Ceolfrid for two centuries, it suffered from Danes about 860 and from Malcolm of Scotland after the Conquest. Then was restored only as a cell of Durham cathedral priory, held by very few monks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-westminster-a:
Westminster Abbey is the most famous of all English abbeys, within the Royal Palace of Westminster's precincts, like Holyrood in Scotland and the Escurial in Spain. On the Thames's northern side a mile or two above ancient London, on a site formerly called Thorney, Isle of Thorns. Its foundation date is quite uncertain: Bede, dying in 736, never mentions it.

It is tolerably certain, however, that a monastery existed by the eighth century. King Offa's charter of 785 first calls it Westminster, to distinguish it from St Paul's minster to the east, and King Edgar's tenth-century charter defines its property bounds. William of Malmesbury says Dunstan brought twelve Glastonbury Benedictines about 960, though that statement is doubted. Whatever its beginnings, an important church and Benedictine community certainly stood there when Edward the Confessor began building, and later sections follow its monks' dispersal under Henry VIII.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-widukind-of-c:
Widukind of Corvey was a tenth-century Saxon historian in Corvey's Benedictine abbey. Unlike earlier chroniclers he did not start from the Roman Empire but from his nation's primitive history. With much enthusiasm he retells tribal sagas, describes heathen ancestors battling Franks.

Narrates Christianity's introduction, then shows Christian Saxons conquering all other nations, including Franks, under Henry I, holding supremacy victoriously despite tribal revolts under Otto, and finally ruling all Christendom. His work became very popular, but brevity and imitation of classical writers, especially Sallust, often make him impossible to understand. It holds great value as often the sole authority for its events and as truthful, reliable portraiture within Saxony's range. What lay outside Saxony passed his comprehension, his view of Otto is incorrect, and he says nothing of Magdeburg's archdiocese or of the pope.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-bede-:
William Bede Dalley was a Sydney lawyer and statesman who became the leading lay voice of Australian Catholics. Born in Sydney in 1831, he died there in 1888. He studied in part at Saint Mary's College, Sydney, and was called to the Bar in 1856. A year later he entered the first parliament chosen under responsible government in New South Wales. He served as solicitor-general in 1858 and 1859 and attorney-general in 1875 to 1877 and 1883 to 1885.

As acting premier after Khartoum fell in 1885, Dalley sent nine hundred men to the Sudan to back imperial troops. He turned down a knighthood and the chief justiceship of New South Wales, yet in 1887 he joined the Privy Council, the first Australian so honoured. Known for courtroom and parliamentary eloquence and a gift for letters, he left newspaper pieces and sketches reprinted in 1866 in Barton's Poets and Prose Writers of New South Wales.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-bentn:
William Bentney, alias Bennet, was an English Jesuit who laboured on the underground mission for four decades and died in prison. Born in Cheshire in 1609, he died on 30 October 1692. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1630 and reached the English mission in 1640, working there with zeal and success for forty-two years. A nobleman whose sisters received sacraments from him had him arrested, and officers carried him to Leicester jail.

No local witness would testify, so he was moved to Derby, tried at the spring assizes of 1682, and sentenced to death. The sentence hung uncarried out for unknown reasons, and James II freed him on taking the throne. After the Revolution he was seized again, tried, and condemned a second time, but that sentence too stayed suspended, and he died in Leicester jail in 1692.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-georg:
William George McCloskey was Bishop of Louisville from 1868 until his death in 1909, and the builder of its churches and schools. Born at Brooklyn in 1823, youngest of five brothers, he studied at Mount Saint Mary's from 1835 and took orders in New York in 1852. He taught moral theology, Scripture, and Latin at his old seminary for about six years, then became first rector of the American College at Rome in 1859.

As rector through the Civil War he held a divided college together despite faction and empty coffers. Arriving in Louisville in late summer 1868, he found sixty-four churches and left one hundred and sixty-five. He raised priests from eighty to two hundred, and brought in Passionists, Benedictines, Sisters of Mercy, and other orders. School pupils grew from two thousand to twelve thousand, and he founded Preston Park Seminary in 1869 and attended the Vatican Council in 1870.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-jewet:
William Jewett Tenney was an American editor and author who built Appleton's Annual Cyclopaedia. Born at Newport, Rhode Island, in 1814, he died at Newark, New Jersey, in 1883. He graduated from Yale in 1832, tried medicine, then law, opening a New York office, before turning to journalism on the Journal of Commerce and the Evening Post in the 1840s. In 1853 he joined D. Appleton and Company as editor.

For Appleton, Tenney began the Annual Cyclopaedia in 1861 and compiled it until his death. He indexed Benton's Abridgment of the Debates of Congress and added a sixteenth volume, and edited Queens of England in 1852. He wrote a Military and Naval History of the Rebellion in 1865 plus a Grammatical Analysis in 1866. A Catholic convert, he married Sarah Brownson, daughter of Orestes Brownson, and held local offices at Elizabeth, New Jersey, including port collector under Buchanan.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-of-ra: William of Ramsey was a monk of Crowland Abbey who flourished about 1219 and wrote lives of saints, some in verse. Born at Ramsey, he is often confused with William of Crowland, Abbot of Ramsey and later of Cluny, who died in 1179. His verified works include a poem on the translation of Saint Guthlac, a prose account of Saint Neot's translation, and a prose life of Saint Waltheof. Lives of Saints Fremund, Edmund the King, and Birinus are also ascribed to him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wilton-abbey:
Wilton Abbey was a Wiltshire nunnery near Salisbury, famed as Edith's home. Earl Wulstan founded a college of priests about 773, but after his death in 800 his widow Saint Alburga turned it into a twelve-nun convent and joined it. Egbert's consent makes him first founder. After beating the Danes at Wilton in 871, Alfred founded a palace-site convent for twenty-six nuns and joined the older house to it.

Wilton's glory is Edith, child of Edgar's handfast union with Wulfrid, a veiled lady he carried off from Wilton in 961. Wulfrid refused marriage and retired with Edith to Wilton, where the girl took the veil as a child from Ethelwold. She refused three abbacies at fifteen, built Denis church and died aged twenty-three in 984. Her feast falls on 16 September. The last abbess, Cecily Bodenham, surrendered the house in March 1539 to William Herbert, who raised Wilton House on its site.
days-with-sir-roger-de-coverley:
Joseph Addison and Richard Steele created Sir Roger de Coverley in the Spectator papers of the early eighteenth century, and Days with Sir Roger gathers the essays of one country visit. The Spectator narrator accepts his friend's invitation to spend a month at Sir Roger's Worcestershire estate. Sir Roger is a kindly, eccentric old knight. His household of aged servants has grown old alongside him.

Essays follow the household member by member, from the butler to the groom. Will Wimble, a cheerful younger son with little to do, gets his own portrait. A picture gallery, a country Sunday at church, and a fox hunt fill the days. The county assizes and the return to London close the visit. Together the pieces form a gentle, funny portrait of English country life and manners.
dead-men-s-money:
A murder mystery set in Berwick-upon-Tweed fills J. S. Fletcher's novel of 1920. Thirty-seven chapters carry the hunt from a one-eyed man to a dark pool. The narrator first saw the man with a black patch over one eye from his mother's front parlour window, ten years before he tells it.

John Phillips is found murdered, and an inquest, parish registers, and a brass-bound chest follow. A salmon gaff, an ice axe, and the motto of the Carstairs family serve as clues. One man reads his own obituary in the papers. A castaway on a raft, waving to an ugly ship, tells part of the buried past. Fletcher keeps the chain of clues tight to the end.
don-rodriguez-chronicles-of-shadow-valle:
Lord Dunsany's Don Rodriguez: Chronicles of Shadow Valley opens with the author's confession about dates. After long research he cannot give the exact period. Magic, even in small quantities, affects time as acids affect metals. The chronicles fall, he can say only, in Spain's Golden Age, toward its later years. Don Rodriguez, a young hidalgo with a sword, a mandolin, and no fortune, rides out to seek adventures worthy of his ancestors. His squire Morano, fat, faithful, and hungry, attends him with a frying pan among his weapons.

Inside, the pair pass inn, forest, and enchanted valley toward the wars Rodriguez hopes will make his name. A magician's house and a princess's sorrow supply the faery. Readers get the Irish fantasist's most sustained romance here, by the man who taught modern fantasy its accent.
fletcher-of-madeley:
Fletcher of Madeley, by Brigadier Margaret Allen of the Salvation Army, tells the life of John Fletcher, the Methodist vicar of Madeley. Allen published the biography at the Salvation Army Printing Works at St Albans. Her contents begin at a castle and a manor house. Early adventures and a sweet girlhood follow. They arrive at a new life given up to the fight. The subject is turned from his home for his faith.

Fletcher himself enters as the Tern Hall tutor, then takes the living of Madeley and alarms his parish with his sermons. Later chapters cover scanty encouragements, an orphan home, sanctified letter writing, the College of Trevecca in Wales, a pen of power, and failing health. Fletcher was John Wesley's chosen successor and the great defender of Methodist doctrine. Allen writes for the holiness movement that claimed him: a scholar saint of the Shropshire iron country.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-LevisonStanley_:
Harold Weisberg wrote this letter on May 19, 1991, to Chauncey Eskridge, a lawyer who had represented Martin Luther King Jr. Weisberg enclosed a Justice Department record concerning Stanley Levison, a close adviser to King. The letter also discusses Weisberg's freedom-of-information lawsuits and his book 'Frame-Up,' about the King assassination.

Weisberg spent years suing for the government's King and Kennedy files, then sharing what he won with other researchers. This letter is part of that traffic: a record passed to a lawyer who had stood near the events. It shows the paper network that kept assassination research moving, letter by letter, before the internet.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-McGuireMickey_M: Marsha Vande Berg interviewed James Earl Ray, the convicted killer of Martin Luther King Jr., and the interview ran under the headline 'Hinted Break Interest to Interviewer.' A Ray interview was a rare get: Ray rarely spoke on the record after his guilty plea. The file preserves the interview under its headline and the interviewer's name, but gives no date or summary of what Ray said.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WadeNey_Wade_Ne: An FBI memorandum dated December 4, 1963, records a talk involving Ney Wade, as reported by Special Agent Eckenrode. It was written less than two weeks after the Kennedy assassination, when field offices were filing reports at full speed. The memo's exact subject stays inside the bureau's terse style. It stands as one of thousands of small reports from that frantic first month.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_foia_The:
The film VICE, nominated for eight Academy Awards including best picture, dramatized Dick Cheney's rise to power. On screen it showed several real documents obtained through freedom of information requests. This briefing book, posted in February 2019, gathers that declassified Cheney file.

Pairing a movie with its source paper is unusual. It lets viewers check Hollywood's version of the vice president against records the government actually released. For the Archive, the film was also proof of concept: documents won through FOIA could end up projected in theaters, shaping how millions picture a recent vice president.
green-valley:
Katharine Reynolds wrote Green Valley, copyrighted in 1919, to cure a heartache. Her author's note tells how, traveling in South America, she grew homesick for the little home towns of her own country, and wrote the book to ease the longing. She dedicates it to all the little one-horse towns where life is sweet and roomy and old-fashioned, where neighbors really neighbor. The first chapters are East and West, Spring in Green Valley, and The Last of the Churchills.

Green Valley is a small American town drawn with love: its church folk, its old families, its seasons of sun and rain and work. The tale moves gently among its people, with courtship and kindness in place of sensation. Reynolds writes as an exile who knows the worth of home. The book is a warm period piece of small-town fiction.
hetty-wesley:
Arthur Quiller-Couch built this novel around Hetty Wesley and her kin. The tale opens far off, at Surat, with a man of the East India Company. It then settles into the Wesley home in England. Hetty, bright and bold, chafes under a strict father's rule.

Across four books, love, shame, and family honor press on Hetty. In one key scene she vows to wed any honest man who will take her. Her sister Molly watches, torn and helpless. Quiller-Couch turns a sad true-life tale into a full novel of pride, faith, and a ruined name.
i-and-my-chimney:
Herman Melville made a comic essay out of a farmhouse chimney in I and My Chimney. The narrator and his great central chimney, two grey-headed old smokers, live in the country. The chimney takes precedence in everything. It greets travelers first, receives guests, and occupies the middle of the house. Its owner keeps the corners. Melville builds the joke patiently, brick by brick, into a portrait of stubborn contentment.

Behind the humor sits a quarrel with improvement: reformers and his own wife would remodel the old pile, and the narrator will not move. The essay, from his Piazza Tales period, turns architecture into character. Readers who think Melville only tragic should meet this genial, immovable householder, defending his chimney like a creed.
in-defence-of-harriet-shelley:
Mark Twain wrote this essay as a courtroom defence of Percy Shelley's first wife against the verdict of Professor Dowden's Life of Shelley. For six years, he says, he had lived in ignorance of the charge that Harriet Shelley was unfaithful and that her guilt drove the poet to desert her for Mary Godwin. He learned that Dowden's book was accepted and taught in American girls' colleges, and took up the case.

Twain examines the evidence the way a lawyer examines a hostile witness. He retells the marriage, the desertion, and Harriet's death, and charges Dowden with constructing a romantic historical fable and adorning it as fact. The essay runs long and hot, with comic set pieces interrupting the indictment. It is Twain the advocate at full stretch, defending a woman sixty years in her grave.
in-the-valley:
Harold Frederic set In the Valley in New York's Mohawk Valley, with copyright in 1890. He dedicated the tale to a venerable friend he calls the foremost citizen of New York State. The valley's Dutch and English families supply its cast. Abraham Ten Broeck appears as a merchant of grave authority.

Ten Broeck steps into a heated quarrel and asks if the men are well advised. His calm hushes the room in that scene. Old feuds, love, and the coming Revolution press on the young narrator. Frederic blends local memory with a tale of a valley on the edge of war.
judith-of-the-godless-valley:
Judith of the Godless Valley is a novel by Honoré Willsie, dated 1922 in its title pages. Nineteen chapters tell the story, from Lost Chief Schoolhouse to Home. Lost Chief is a valley where, one winter Sunday, a sermon is preached for the first time in nearly ten years. Everyone who can move heads for the schoolhouse.

The book opens with a saying from the Reverend James Fowler about preaching without fear or favor. Chapter titles promise a graduation dance, a rodeo, wild horses, and a log chapel. A first sermon, the battle of the bulls, and a flame in the valley follow. Douglas Spencer rides through the opening scene. Willsie sets faith against a rough, godless valley in her Western tale.
lives-of-the-english-poets-waller-milton:
Johnson treats Waller, Milton, and Cowley in this 1891 Cassell volume. The introduction recalls Johnson, born at Lichfield in 1709. He was sixty-eight when booksellers engaged him for the Lives. He called them little lives and prefaces to a little edition.

The bargain, made on Easter Eve 1777, troubled his conscience. London publishers wanted to answer an Edinburgh poets edition. They called that rival printing inaccurate and small-typed. Johnson's prefaces grew into the most famous literary biographies in English. Edward Dilly, a contracting bookseller, told Boswell the bargain's history. Bell's London sales of the Edinburgh edition provoked the project.
locusts-and-wild-honey:
John Burroughs gathers nature essays in this fourth writings volume. His preface admits the title works as allegory, not description. Locusts and wild honey suggest nature's free, ungarnered harvests. Observing eyes and ears gather that harvest everywhere, he writes.

The Pastoral Bees opens a contents list rich in birds. Sharp Eyes, Strawberries, and Speckled Trout follow in season. Birds'-Nesting and The Halcyon in Canada close the essays. Fuertes drew the whip-poor-will illustration for the volume. Gleason photographed trout streams and yellow birches for it. Esopus-on-Hudson signs Burroughs's preface to the collection.
luther-table-talk-selections-bell-morley:
Students at Luther's dinner table in Wittenberg scribbled down whatever the great man said, and the Table Talk preserves those evenings. The Bell and Morley selections, from 1886, gather his talk on theology, the devil, marriage, beer, and the Pope. Unguarded Luther fills every page.

Funny, furious, tender, and profane by turns, he judges princes and praises his wife within a single supper. The sayings were never meant for print, which is their charm and their caution. Historians handle them as reported speech, but the voice rings true. No formal treatise gives so human a portrait of the reformer. Readers finish the selections feeling they have actually sat in that crowded, smoky room.
mrs-shelley:
Lucy Madox Rossetti wrote this life of Mary Shelley in 1890. It came out in the Eminent Women series. Rossetti thanks past Shelley scholars, her husband among them. She says new papers on Mary's later years were lent to her.

Letters to Trelawny came from his kin as early as 1888. She used Dowden's Life of Shelley and Godwin lives as sources. Her rule was to print no claim without a document behind it. The book shows Mary as daughter, wife, widow, and working writer. V1 praised its sympathy for a woman who bore scandal and grief with courage.
my-lady-s-money:
Wilkie Collins calls this tale an episode in the life of a young girl. Lady Lydiard, a lord's widow, opens the story by her fireside. Three old letters lie open on her lap. Her adopted daughter Isabel Miller shares the cast list.

Other figures include a steward, a lawyer, and a nephew named Felix Sweetsir. Old Sharon works in the byways of legal Bohemia. Even Lady Lydiard's dog Tommie earns a place in the list. Part one is called The Disappearance. V1 says a stolen banknote drives the mystery. Collins spins love, theft, and suspicion into a light, quick tale.
nightmare-abbey:
Thomas Love Peacock published Nightmare Abbey in London in 1818, naming himself only as the author of Headlong Hall. A verse from Butler heads the tale, about a dark lantern of the spirit. Those who bear it, Butler says, see visions in the dark and rack their own minds.

Dialogue on melancholy opens the sampled pages, with sonnets written at a sitting. Matthew praises fine melancholy as the breed of perfect wit. Stephen loves such things out of measure, and asks for a stool to be melancholy upon. Peacock mocks the gloomy young men of his day. The copy also adds notes to the tale at the back.
no-and-other-stories-compiled-by-uncle-h:
Uncle Humphrey compiled No and Other Stories in 1851 for young readers. His preface says the little book aims at both instruction and amusement. He hopes his dear young friends will profit by its perusal. It will show them their duty, he promises, and lead them to do it.

The little word No, he writes, matters greatly though it has but two letters. Saying it keeps children from the path of sin and misery. Stories urge charity to the destitute, as little Willy showed. Good sons and daughters comfort their parents, in sickness or in health. Forgiveness, the preface adds, is an attribute of Heaven.
no-breakfast-plan-fasting-cure-dewey:
Doctor Edward Hooker Dewey argued that skipping breakfast could cure much illness. His book The No Breakfast Plan and the Fasting-Cure states that case at length. Dewey served as a physician in the Civil War era.

He claims that hunger rests the body and lets it heal itself. Case tales fill the book: patients who fasted and felt reborn. He attacks the habit of eating on a fixed clock. Modern readers will find some advice dated and risky. Yet the book helped launch the fasting movement that still thrives in health circles today.
notes-to-the-complete-poetical-works-of-:
Mary W. Shelley wrote these notes for the complete poetical works of her husband, Percy Bysshe Shelley. Her preface belongs to the first collected edition of 1839. Obstacles had long blocked a perfect edition, she says. With them at last removed, she hastens to fulfil an important duty.

That duty is twofold: print the poems with all possible correctness, and tell how each was made. The poems sprang, living and warm, from his heart and brain, she writes. She refuses to colour the truth about his private life. His errors, she argues, may be fearlessly avowed, since impartial judgment would brighten his character. Her notes tie poems to their making.
observations-and-reflections-made-in-the:
Hester Lynch Piozzi published volume one of her Observations and Reflections in London in 1789. Strahan and Cadell printed her two volumes on France, Italy, and Germany. Her preface reaches back to Rome for a figure of speech. Certain men there, the Preciae, walked before a priest's procession, bidding folk leave work or play.

Prefaces, she jokes, can hope for little better usage than those heralds got. Her book proclaims the approach of much that has passed before, in greater splendour. Still, she hopes for a moment's amusement for her countrymen. The work also carries her thanks to foreign friends whose tenderness softened the sorrows of absence.
observations-by-mr-dooley:
Finley Peter Dunne wrote Observations by Mr Dooley as a run of short essays under one comic voice. A little essay on books opens the list. The law's delays, Sherlock Holmes, and international amenities follow. Art patronage, immigration, and White House discipline show the range of the talk.

Money and matrimony, Prince Henry's visit, and Cuba against beet sugar appear in turn. Bad men from the West, the Philippine peace, and King Edward's coronation date the set. One advantage of poverty and the fighting word sit among graver heads. Rights and privileges of women, hypocrisy, history, and gratitude close the contents. Mr Dooley comments on America at table talk pace.
other-people-s-money:
Émile Gaboriau, the French pioneer of the detective novel, opens Other People's Money in the Marais. The Rue Saint-Gilles is its quietest street. Everyone knows everyone there, and gossip flourishes like grass. On the afternoon of April 27, 1872, a servant in striped waistcoat and white apron goes from door to door asking questions, and the whole street wonders who he is looking for.

He claims to be gathering references for his cousin, a cook about to take a place nearby. Then comes the question that matters: do you know M. Vincent Favoral? The concierges know no one better. Gaboriau builds his mystery of Parisian finance and family honor out of such doorstep inquiries, in the manner that taught a generation of crime writers their trade.
percy-bysshe-shelley: The hosted sample stops at the front matter of John Addington Symonds's life of Percy Bysshe Shelley, the title page, contents, and list of authorities, with no chapter text visible. The book belongs to the English Men of Letters series, edited by John Morley. Its chapters run from birth and childhood through Eton and Oxford, two marriages, Marlow, Italy, and Pisa to the last days, and the authorities list Mrs. Shelley's edition of the works, Hogg's life, and Trelawny's records.
pixy-s-holiday-journey:
George Lang's Pixy's Holiday Journey, translated from the German by Mary E. Ireland in 1906, is a children's story about three boys and their dog Pixy. Ireland dedicated her translation to two boys who had taken keen pleasure in hearing the manuscript read aloud.

Twelve chapters follow the holiday trip. The boys meet a kind friend, stay at the Swan Inn, spend a whole day sightseeing, and visit the zoological gardens. Trouble comes in turns: Fritz in trouble, then Pixy in trouble, then Pixy's earnings, a visit to a clothing mouse, and a night in a deserted cabin. The last chapter calls the journey a well-spring of pleasure, which sums up the book's cheerful tone.
raabe-the-black-galley:
A mysterious black ship strikes the Spanish in the Dutch war of independence, and Raabe builds his novella The Black Galley around her. Presented here in English, the tale centers on a black-hulled vessel that seems to appear from nowhere in the night sea battles. Freedom, not plunder, is her cargo and her cause.

Part historical adventure and part meditation on liberty, the story shows Raabe turning the past into gripping narrative. Dutch sailors and Spanish pursuers fill the decks with period life. The galley's secret gives the tale its engine of suspense. Germany's great storyteller of the 1800s rarely wrote anything more stirring at this length. The novella remains his most popular short work abroad.
rainbow-valley: Rainbow Valley, by Lucy Maud Montgomery, author of Anne of Green Gables, is dedicated to the memory of Goldwin Lapp, Robert Brookes, and Morley Shier, who died in the war. Only the contents are shown. The chapters follow the Ingleside children and the manse children. Mary Vance arrives and stays at the manse. The manse girls clean house. A dreadful discovery follows. The good-conduct club appears. Faith makes a friend.
red-money:
Fergus Hume, author of The Mystery of a Hansom Cab, published this mystery in 1911. Its contents promise secrets from the first: The Drama of Little Things, In the Wood, and An Unexpected Recognition. Two chapters pair The Woman and the Man, in both orders, hinting at a bond under strain.

Later titles bring a secretary, a midnight scene, and then blackmail in plain words. A conspiracy follows, and Miss Greeby turns detective in chapter fourteen. Guesswork, the last straw, and a trail close the list printed here. Hume, a master of the light mystery, sets money, secrecy, and pursuit turning against each other.
reminiscences-of-samuel-taylor-coleridge:
Joseph Cottle, who had known both poets in their youth, wrote these reminiscences of Samuel Taylor Coleridge and Robert Southey. His introduction is solemn: he has outlived nearly all the friends of his early days. Nearer eighty than seventy, he looks back on a past that seems like the tumult of a dream.

Cottle refuses to merely praise Coleridge's eloquence and forget his failings. No lesson for later readers would come from such homage, he argues. Lessons lie in every feature of Coleridge's mind and every part of his eventful, checkered life. He calls Coleridge the most singular man this country produced in the past century.
roast-beef-medium-the-business-adventure:
Edna Ferber tells the business adventures of Emma McChesney in these stories, with twenty-seven pictures by James Montgomery Flagg. A foreword plays with the title before any tale begins. Roast Beef, Medium, it says, is not only a food but a philosophy of life.

At life's dining table, the foreword runs, a soft voice urges tongue in aspic, chicken pie, or eggs Benedictine on the diner. Plain roast beef sounds prosaic beside such viands in frilly paper trousers. Yet the fancy dishes burn the tongue, and the check appals. The safe, sane, and sure choice, the foreword argues, beats the tempting dish in the end.
secret-history-revealed-by-lady-peggy-o-:
C. N. and A. M. Williamson published this novel in 1915, with a color front plate by Clarence Rowe. The Williamsons had written The Lightning Conductor Discovers America and Lady Betty Across the Water. Lady Peggy O'Malley tells the tale in her own voice.

Peggy insists that only she, Diana, Major Vandyke, and Captain Eagleston March know the full truth. Presidents and war chiefs know the public half, while Peggy holds the private half. She traces how vast events grew from tiny starts. Love, duty, and wartime secrets drive a brisk tale told with wit and charm.
shelley:
Sydney Waterlow published this short life and study of Shelley with T. C. and E. C. Jack in London in 1913. Contents divide the poet's story into his age, his chief writings, and his triple fame as poet of rebellion, of nature, and of love. A note on books about Shelley closes the volume.

Waterlow opens with a puzzle: Shelley stirs love and hate as a man, apart from his art. Admirers hail him as a banner of freedom, torn but flying. Canon makers have daubed him with false sainthood, Waterlow warns. His pages seek the engaging, flawed person behind the legend and the lyrics.
stories-from-the-odyssey:
H. L. Havell, once a scholar of University College, Oxford, retold Stories from the Odyssey in plain prose, following his similar books on Herodotus, Greek tragedy, the Aeneid, and the Iliad. Lines from Tennyson stand at the front, praising the man whose will stays strong under suffering.

The contents track Homer's poem in order. They start with Telemachus, Penelope, and the suitors. They follow the visits to Nestor at Pylos and to Sparta. They reach Odysseus with Calypso and among the Phaeacians. Then come the wanderings and the visit to Hades. The Sirens, Scylla and Charybdis, and the isle of the sun follow. The landing in Ithaca and the meeting with the swineherd Eumaeus bring the hero home.
the-boy-scouts-of-the-geological-survey:
Scout Master Robert Shaler wrote The Boy Scouts of the Geological Survey. Its chapters start with The Golden Feather and a fight on a cliff. A night in the woods, friends at a farm, and a night guest come next. Then the boys turn scout detectives and join a surveying squad. Camp life, a new project, and the result of the surveys close the list.

The tale opens on Ralph Kenyon, a young trapper at work in the wilds. He ties a limp mink to his pack-saddle and resets the trap, in hope of its larger mate. His horse Keno bears the load of pelts. Ralph tells Keno to browse on young cottonwoods while he does his sums. From a worn book he lists the take: one mink, six coon, three skunk, a gray fox, and seventeen rabbit skins.
the-chums-of-scranton-high-at-ice-hockey: Donald Ferguson wrote this boys' school story, copyrighted in 1919 by the World Syndicate Publishing Company of Cleveland and New York. Only the title page and contents are present here. The chapters follow the Scranton boys through a hockey match with a scratch seven, startling news from Thad, a mother's sacrifice, games with Keyport and Belleville, and a wonderful discovery. A boy named Nick runs through the titles, getting a chance, being encouraged, and making good at the end. No chapter text follows.
the-desert-valley: Jackson Gregory, author of The Bells of San Juan and Man to Man, published The Desert Valley with Hodder and Stoughton of London and Charles Scribner's Sons in 1921. Its contents list twenty-six chapters, from A Bluebird's Feather and Superstition Pool through Payment in Raw Gold, The Golden Secret, and Howard Holds the Gulch, to a close called When Day Dawned. An opening head, The Desert, begins over the regions of the southwestern desert country of Arizona. Only the front matter, contents, and that opening line are present here.
the-golden-key:
George MacDonald wrote this small, bright tale in 1867, and many hold it his most fine fairy tale. It here stands in the text of its Wikisource form, from an old print. MacDonald was a Scots priest whose tales veil deep faith in the garb of fairy lore.

A boy finds a golden key at the end of a rainbow, in a wood at dusk. He joins a girl on a quest for the lock the key fits, up a stair of light and shade. Pure and brief, the tale is Victorian fantasy at its most clear and true.
the-home-in-the-valley:
Emilie F. Carlen wrote The Home in the Valley. Elbert Perce translated it from the original Swedish. Charles Scribner published it in New York in 1854. Carlen is named as the author of One Year of Wedlock. A translator's preface opens the volume. Perce notes that Carlen was little known in the country a few years earlier.

The marked success of One Year of Wedlock changed that, Perce says. Its success encouraged him to present more of her works. He praises her range across books. One book revels in home scenes and characters. Another book turns to startling, melodramatic events. He compares that second manner to modern French romance writers.
the-lily-of-the-valley:
Honore de Balzac dedicated his novel to Doctor J. B. Nacquart, whose science once saved his life, and Katharine Prescott Wormeley translated it into English. Felix de Vandenesse opens the tale in a letter to Countess Natalie de Manerville. She has demanded the history of his past life.

Felix warns her that a phantom shadows his happiness and that solemn memories lie buried in his soul. Jealous questions from Natalie force the story out of him. Readers receive a confession of youthful love for a married countess in the Touraine countryside, told with Balzac care for place and feeling.
the-longest-journey:
E. M. Forster's The Longest Journey is divided into three parts named for places: Cambridge, Sawston, and Wiltshire. Part one opens among Cambridge students arguing philosophy over a carpet. Ansell lights matches and insists that a cow in the meadow is there whether anyone looks at her or not. His friends push back: has he proved it, or only proved it to himself?

The talk turns on whether objects exist only when someone sees them, or have a real existence of their own. Forster uses the familiar, solid cow to make the puzzle of objectivity and subjectivity manageable. The scene sets an intellectual, questioning tone, with young men testing ideas against each other before the story widens to the other two places.
the-lost-valley: J. M. Walsh's The Lost Valley was published in Melbourne by the C. J. DeGaris Publishing House in 1921. Only front matter has come down here — the title page and contents — so none of the novel can be read. The contents divide it into two parts: Part I, The Posthumous Puzzle of Mr. Bryce, with chapters on strange behaviour, a thief in the night, and circumstantial evidence; and Part II, The Adventures of Mr. Abel Cumshaw, with a pursuit, a hidden valley, and an expiation among its chapter titles.
the-minute-boys-of-the-mohawk-valley: James Otis wrote The Minute Boys of the Mohawk Valley, a boys' Revolutionary War novel illustrated by A. Burnham Shute and published in 1911. Only the title page, contents, and list of illustrations are present here, so the story itself does not appear. The chapters promise young soldiers, a powwow, an ambush, prisoners, and an escape, then a fort assault, mutiny, and torture. Illustration captions show an Indian striding into an encampment and hundreds of Indians dancing around a huge fire.
the-scouts-of-the-valley:
Joseph A. Altsheler opens The Scouts of the Valley with a chapter called The Lone Canoe. A light bark canoe moves swiftly up one of the twin streams forming the Ohio. A single human figure sits in it. The water babbles at the edges where it laps the land. In the center the full current flows steadily and without noise.

Early dusk throws thin shadows over the world. One glowing shaft of sunlight pierces the heavy forest. It falls directly on the figure in the boat. The paddler is a boy in years only, Altsheler writes. He swings the great paddle with enviable ease and vigor. His rifle lies beside him, its stock beautifully carved. The boy is Henry Ware, a child of the forest. He holds the canoe steady, listening, then shoots into shadow along the northern shore.
the-second-latchkey: C. N. and A. M. Williamson wrote The Second Latchkey. Doubleday, Page and Company published it at Garden City, New York, in 1920. Rudolph Tandler drew the frontispiece. The pages shown give the title matter and the start of the contents only. No chapter text follows. The first chapters are A White Rose, Smiths and Smiths, and Why She Came. The great moment and the second latchkey itself come next. Later headings name the Countess de Santiago and a blue diamond ring. The thing Knight wanted is also promised.
the-soldier-of-the-valley: Nelson Lloyd wrote The Soldier of the Valley, published by Charles Scribner's Sons in New York in 1904. A. B. Frost illustrated it. The pages shown give the title matter and a list of illustrations only. No chapter text follows. The frontispiece is captioned, They called to me as a boy. Other captions promise a welcome home and a parting from Tim at the ploughs. A tiger story and a last look at Black Log appear in the list. He pumped me dry closes the captions shown.
the-story-of-a-nodding-donkey: Laura Lee Hope's Make Believe story of a nodding donkey was published by Grosset and Dunlap in New York, illustrated by Harry L. Smith. Only the title pages and publisher's lists are present here. The lists place the book among the Make Believe stories. The Sawdust Doll and the Calico Clown stand beside it. The China Cat and the Plush Bear follow. A Bobbsey Twins list comes after. The donkey's own adventures do not appear.
the-story-of-the-odyssey: The Reverend Alfred J. Church retells the Odyssey for general readers. He uses eighteen sections. They begin with the counsel of Athene and the assembly at Ithaca. Nestor's and Menelaus's tales follow. Ulysses rides his raft. Nausicaa and the Phaeacians follow. The Cyclops and Circe follow. The dwellings of the dead, the Sirens, and Scylla come next. The return and the hero in his home close the tale. Only the title page and that contents list appear here, with an introduction's heading. Church's retelling itself does not appear.
the-story-of-wellesley:
Florence Converse wrote this history of Wellesley College, opening it with the college song Alma Mater, written by Anne L. Barrett of the class of 1886. Her preface begins the day after the Wellesley fire, when an eager young Boston reporter came by appointment to interview a group of grief-stricken alumnae and teachers.

The reporter arrived with a young man's light-hearted breathlessness. Bernard Shaw and Arnold Bennett fill their plays with such reporters. He called out on the run to the smallest alumna in the group. He cried for pranks with his pencil poised. What she told him is not recorded, Converse adds. It never appeared in his report either. He wrote that report with courtesy and sympathy afterwards. The scene makes a wry opening. A catastrophe's shadow hangs over the college history.
the-tale-of-major-monkey: Arthur Scott Bailey's Major Monkey came out in 1919 from Grosset and Dunlap, illustrated by Lawrence Brehm. Front matter and a contents list are all that this record contains, so the Major's campaign never gets under way. Twenty-two chapters promise strange whispers, a new army, war in the woods, stone throwing, a retreat, and a confession from the Major himself. Chapter titles also mention a tiger supposedly inside a tree and a fast ride, giving the flavor of a comic animal adventure without supplying its pages.
their-wedding-journey:
William Dean Howells published his account of Basil and Isabel March in 1871, following their wedding trip through familiar American places. The contents promise Niagara, the St. Lawrence, Montreal, and a return to Niagara twelve years later. Howells warns that the courtship itself stays mostly offstage.

He says the broken and renewed match in Europe would need a skilled romancer. His own task is plainer scenes of American life seen by newly married travellers. The couple choose a quiet, private journey weeks after the wedding. Readers get landscape sketches, character sketches, and a marriage observed with humour.
theocritus-idylls-calverley:
Theocritus, a Greek poet of the third century BCE, invented pastoral poetry in Sicily and Alexandria. C. S. Calverley translated the Idylls, Epigrams, and Epitaphs into English verse. Shepherds, singers, and lovers fill his short poems.

Herdsmen compete in song, praise patrons, and court reluctant girls. Some idylls move to the city, with housewives gossiping at a festival. The poems mix rustic dialect, humor, and polished artifice. Virgil learned the pastoral form directly from these pieces. Every later shepherd poem, down to Milton, descends from Theocritus. Calverley's verse keeps the charm light and musical.
thucydides-peloponnesian-war-crawley:
Thucydides, an Athenian general exiled in war, wrote the History of the Peloponnesian War. Richard Crawley's translation made it a staple in English. The war set Athens against Sparta for a generation.

Thucydides insists on facts, causes, and the logic of power. Famous speeches frame plague, revolt, and the ruin of expeditions. His account of the Sicilian disaster still chills readers. Scholars call his work the first scientific history. Leaders still study it for its cold lessons on fear, honor, and interest in statecraft. Crawley's version keeps the speeches taut and clear.
uneasy-money:
P. G. Wodehouse opens Uneasy Money outside a London restaurant at lunch time in June. A large, pleasant young man stands frowning in Shaftesbury Avenue. He stays lost in thought while the crowd flows past. He is William FitzWilliam Delamere Chalmers, Lord Dawlish, and he has no secret sorrow. He is only working out how to lay a golf ball dead in front of the Palace Theatre. That game fills his head whenever Claire Fenwick keeps him waiting.

Wodehouse notes that Dawlish once got through nine holes of this mind golf during a single long wait. As he stands there, a shabby street seller edges toward him. The man's tray holds collar studs, laces, and buttonhooks. The scene sets the tone: a kind, simple peer in a city full of sharp eyes. The comedy grows from his good nature meeting people who want something from him.
up-the-chimney:
Shepherd Knapp wrote Up the Chimney as a Christmas play for children. Before the curtain rises, Mother Goose steps out and speaks to the audience directly. She promises a play set on Christmas Eve, in the home of a doctor and his wife, with their little girl and boy. The children are busy writing letters, the mother knits, and the father reads his newspaper, while cold weather presses outside.

The first scene then shows that room, with a fireplace and stockings hung beside it, and a dark window at the back. The girl is Polly, and her brother Jack speaks first, asking his mother how to spell the word friend. Knapp frames the whole piece as a story told to child viewers, who are asked to sit quiet and watch. The play mixes home life, letter writing, and Christmas wonder for a young audience.
vivian-grey:
Benjamin Disraeli published Vivian Grey in 1826 and 1827, and a publisher's note at the front of this edition places him among the novelists of the early nineteenth century. The note calls Vivian Grey and Sybil, from 1845, the start and end of his truly creative period. His late books, Lothair in 1870 and Endymion in 1880, add little, it says, beyond the changes that old age brings to feeling and power.

Disraeli's period, the note argues, was that of Bulwer, Dickens, Thackeray, and the later Scott, though his fame as a statesman in his last decade tends to hide the fact. He was born in 1804 and died in 1881. The book appears here as part of The English Comedie Humaine, second series. Readers meet the first novel of a man who would lead a government, written when its author was barely out of his teens.
